documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into strategic command reconstitutes rather than augments command judgement, placing systematic pressure on what Clausewitz identified as the essential intelligence of command: coup d’œil, the cultivated capacity for rapid holistic synthesis that distinguishes the formed commander from the competent administrator. This article argues that command intuition develops through practice and is sustained through experience, yet three compounding pathologies in AI-augmented environments progressively erode its development and exercise. Drawing on Clausewitz’s analytical framework, the article identifies these pathologies as automation bias, which substitutes deference for judgement; algorithmic monoculture, which collapses cognitive diversity through which actors recognise what shared models cannot perceive; and delegated infopolitik, which embeds consequential political choices within system architecture, rendering them invisible to commanders and severing the accountability chain that war as an act of policy requires.

Digital transformation is changing the occupations that graduates can enter, yet little is known about which digital occupations Cambodian university students favor. Preference ratings for 26 digital occupations were collected from 335 respondents at BELTEI International University through a five-point questionnaire with good internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = .879). Means and standard deviations ranked the occupations, independent samples t tests compared gender and type of institution, and one-way analyses of variance compared major of study, area of expertise, age group, and position. All occupations were rated favorably (M = 3.81 to 4.18). Electro technology engineers, digital marketing and strategy specialists, and system engineers ranked highest, whereas FinTech engineers and artificial intelligence and machine learning specialists ranked lowest. Area of expertise differed significantly for 24 occupations, age group for 18, and major of study for 15, and 40 of the 66 significant results remained significant after a Bonferroni adjustment. Gender, type of institution, and position produced only a few small differences that did not survive the adjustment. The findings suggest that universities should differentiate digital course offerings and career counseling by professional background and age, and should expose students to the data-intensive occupations in which interest was lowest. The cross-sectional, single-institution design limits generalization, and later studies should add post hoc tests, multiple institutions, and measures of the factors behind preference.

Purpose This paper systematically reviews empirical literature on job quality (JQ) in developed economies. Based on 40 articles spanning over 25 years, we analyse the key definitions, theories, methods, measures and outcomes associated with JQ in developed economies. Design/methodology/approach In conducting the review, we followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Our initial search yielded 9262 published records. Based on inclusion criteria, 40 articles were included in this review. These papers were published between 1999 and 2025, across 31 journals. Most studies were published after 2010 in management, industrial relations and health-related journals. Findings We reveal inconsistencies and problems with existing approaches, and make conceptual, theoretical and methodological contributions. Finally, we develop a research agenda to inform and improve future studies related to JQ, and advance the literature and policymaking. Research limitations/implications In terms of possible limitations regarding these findings, restricting the review to Q1 journal could potentially bias the results and the inclusion of only English-language studies could inadvertently exclude valuable research published in other languages. Practical implications The findings will enable researchers to better plan and design future research. This research will usefully inform policymaking directed towards improving JQ and subsequently benefiting workers, organisations, economies and societies. Social implications Advancing theoretical and empirical knowledge regarding JQ will enable the creation and maintenance of better jobs and thereby improve social and economic outcomes, including health and wellbeing and social mobility. Originality/value Extending beyond the narrow foci of previous JQ reviews, this review identifies gaps and inconsistencies in JQ research and generates conceptual, theoretical and methodological contributions. Subsequently, it develops a future research agenda designed to enable researchers to better plan and design research, and inform policymaking.

Generative artificial intelligence is now widely used in higher education. It increasingly performs the academic tasks through which students have traditionally judged their own ability. Yet studies of the relationship between perceived generative AI capability and academic self-efficacy report positive, negative, and non-significant results, and the divergence appears even within a single meta-analysis. This critical review treats the contradiction as a question about a conditional relationship. What decides the direction of the association is not perceived AI capability itself but how students integrate it into their learning. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, social comparison theory, and self-regulated learning theory, the review examines 22 studies and proposes two competing pathways. In the enabling pathway, higher self-regulated learning may allow perceived AI capability to function as a learning resource that supports mastery and the development of competence. In the undermining pathway, lower self-regulated learning may turn the same perception into a source of cognitive offloading, AI dependence, and unfavorable competence comparison. Self-regulated learning is therefore treated as the key boundary condition through which perceived AI capability bears on academic self-efficacy. Within the studies reviewed, each pathway has support on its own. Their coexistence, however, has not been explained within a single framework, and the moderating role of self-regulated learning has not been directly tested. The review states three testable propositions on this basis and outlines how future research could test them.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) has entered a therapeutic era in which priorities extend beyond detecting steatosis to identifying treatment-actionable fibrosis, rationalising referral and biopsy, standardising trial endpoints and monitoring response. Artificial intelligence (AI) spans electronic health records, non-invasive tests, imaging and digital pathology, but reports often omit the user, threshold and consequence. We conducted a structured narrative review and developed the author-proposed ACTION framework. ACTION comprises attached action, calibration in context, threshold-specific benefit, integration, oversight, and non-discrimination and monitoring. Evidence is uneven. Case-finding and enrichment models can identify uncoded or higher-risk patients, but their prospective effects on testing, referral and outcomes remain unproven. Imaging AI supports reproducible quantification, although signals may add little beyond clinical variables. The human-reviewed AI-based measurement tool for MASH (in regulatory records) is among the most mature applications reviewed, within a narrowly specified clinical-trial context. It is qualified for specified MASH clinical-trial workflows, not for autonomous diagnosis or unrestricted treatment selection. AI becomes clinically meaningful only when a calibrated output is linked to a predefined action, an accountable human user and a measurable patient or trial outcome.

documents.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within adult continuing education has been observed to be a major contributing factor in the transformation of the conditions under which adults construct their knowledge and professional competencies. This article presents a critical analysis of the existing subject literature, addressing the issue of adult learners' subjectivity in educational environments saturated with GenAI. The analysis adopts a constructivist understanding of learning as an active process of meaning-making based on experience, iteration, and reflection. A particular emphasis is placed on the pedagogical category of error, interpreted within the framework of constructivist theories. A critical analysis was conducted of how GenAI is used in the learning of adult workers, what opportunities and limitations it presents from a constructivist perspective, and what consequences it has for the learner's agency in the context of Industry 5.0. This analysis was based on selected publications. In conclusion, a set of meta-competencies and didactic recommendations was proposed that may help protect the right to make mistakes and preserve the agency of adult learners in the era of algorithmic optimisation.

How do humans recognize and rectify social missteps? We achieve social competence by looking around at our peers, decoding subtle cues from others around us — a raised eyebrow, a laugh — to evaluate the environment and our actions. Robots, however, struggle to perceive and make use of these nuanced reactions. By employing a novel neck-mounted device that records facial expressions from the chin region, we explore the potential of previously untapped data to capture and interpret human responses to robot error. First, we develop NeckNet-18, a 3D facial reconstruction model to map the reactions captured through the chin camera onto facial points and head motion. We then use these facial responses to develop a robot error detection model which outperforms standard methodologies such as using OpenFace or video data, generalizing well especially for within-participant data. Through this work, we argue for expanding human-in-the-loop robot sensing, fostering more seamless integration of robots into diverse human environments, pushing the boundaries of social cue detection and opening new avenues for adaptable robotics.

This study investigated an innovative LLM-powered AI agent in the training of pre-interpreting preparation technique in an undergraduate interpreting course as a discrete language learning context. Over one month, 19 senior English majors engaged with three context-specific AI agents created via a DeepSeek-to-Doubao workflow to deliver a four-tier practice framework aimed at fostering self-regulated learning. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), open-ended survey items, and structured reflection logs. A mixed-methods evaluation revealed overwhelmingly favorable perceptions, driven by compressed preparation time, targeted and automated extraction of terminology and thematic knowledge, and interactive formative feedback. However, the students encountered distinct challenges, including prompt sensitivity, data hallucinations, and speech-recognition inconsistencies. Ultimately, while AI agents served as effective preparatory coaches, successful integration requires a structured verification pedagogy to train students in critical fact-checking and algorithmic boundary navigation.

Background/Objectives: Breast cancer diagnosis from histopathological images must include accurate categorization, reliable uncertainty assessment, comprehensible evidence, and clinically significant reporting. Although deep learning-based histopathological classification has made significant progress, current methods often rely on single-model representations and do not provide sufficient approaches to manage prediction error and incorporate complementary morphological information across geographic scales. Furthermore, categorization, explainability, and clinical reporting are treated as separate tasks, creating a gap between image-level prediction and workflow-based clinical decision support. Methods: In this study, we propose a Task-Delegation Multi-Agent System (MAS) incorporating a Generalist Perception Agent (GPA), a Specialist Perception Agent (SPA), and a Clinical Reasoning Agent (CRA) to address these limitations. The GPA (BreastCareNet-G) handles routine cases using multi-scale CNN feature fusion, while the SPA (BreastCareNet-S) acts as a ViT-based consultant for complex morphological patterns. Instead of simple linear routing, we introduce a confidence-driven delegation protocol (0.85 threshold) where the GPA autonomously escalates ambiguous cases to the SPA. In scenarios of persistent evidence conflict, where both perception agents fail to meet the confidence threshold, the CRA (an LLM-based agent) intervenes to analyze the discrepancy, generate a structured diagnostic summary, and mandate an immediate human-in-the-loop review. Results: An analysis of the publicly available BreaKHis dataset demonstrated that the GPA autonomously accepted 2365 cases with a 99.79% accuracy. Based on raw forced-classification logits, the combined system correctly predicted 2368/2373 cases. For the 8 escalated cases, the SPA functioned as an unvalidated reporting adjunct, generating secondary ViT-based metadata for the CRA rather than extending automated clinical sensitivity. Conclusions: The proposed MAS framework effectively orchestrates multi-scale feature extraction, confidence-guided delegation, explainable AI, and LLM-assisted conflict resolution into a unified diagnostic workflow, serving as a robust technical proof of concept for enhancing the dependability and clinical safety of AI-assisted breast histopathology analysis.

documents.abstract: Nano-enabled drinking water purification technologies have emerged as effective solutions for removing chemical, microbial, and emerging contaminants, particularly in decentralized and resource-limited settings. While existing research predominantly emphasizes material performance, removal efficiency and environmental safety, limited attention has been given to how prolonged reliance on invisible and automated nano-based systems influences human risk perception and behavior over time. This narrative review aimed to examine the potential psychological and behavioral implications of nano-enabled drinking water purification systems and to propose the concept of psychological latency as a framework for understanding long-term cognitive, emotional and behavioral adaptation to nano-enabled water purification technologies. The review concentrates on the purification of drinking water through nanotechnology. However, the psychological mechanisms discussed, such as cognitive offloading, trust transfer, reduced vigilance, and over-reliance, are not distinctive to this technology and may also occur in other automated purification systems. Drawing on environmental risk perception, human–technology interaction, and behavioral adaptation frameworks, this review synthesizes evidence suggesting that trust formation, perceived control and vigilance may represent important mechanisms underlying user experiences with nano-enabled water technologies. The synthesis further highlights potential benefits, including anxiety reduction and behavioral normalization, while also highlighting potential concerns such as over-reliance and risk compensation. By integrating psychological dimensions with material and system-level considerations, this review emphasizes the importance of human-centered design features such as transparency, feedback mechanisms, and risk communication. The findings position psychological risk perception as a critical but underexplored component of responsible nano-enabled water purification deployment and provide a foundation for future empirical research, public health policy development and sustainable water intervention design.

documents.abstract: Organizations increasingly delegate work to AI agents that run on employees' computers, where they read and change files, execute programs and contact external services, while employees paste business and personal data into AI chat services. Operating systems, identity systems and network controls authorize all of this as the employee, because they know no principal smaller than the user. Data protection law, the EU AI Act, sector regulation and the NIST frameworks nonetheless hold the organization accountable for what its AI does, and they call for least privilege, human oversight, the ability to intervene, and records that withstand scrutiny. From these sources we derive six requirements for governing agents on endpoints. We prove that no control deciding by account, role, device or program can enforce a policy that treats an agent differently from its user, whereas attribution along the chain of processes suffices; that the workload of human oversight is bounded by the number of distinct situations, with the probability that the next request needs a person below $K/(en)$ after $n$ requests; and that rarity of unsafe behaviour offers no protection at organizational scale. After assessing the established control families, we present IOArx, which names the agent behind each file operation, decides it by a policy written for agents, holds the agent while a person decides, gates network connections, inspects submissions to AI services and keeps a hash-chained record, all on the device. In measurements, IOArx attributed processes to their agents without a misattribution, held a violating agent on Linux within a median of 3.1~ms, and raised no false alarm on 32{,}771 real prompts.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for writing, retrieval, explanation, planning, tutoring, decision support, and agentic work. Yet much everyday AI use still begins with a familiar interaction pattern: a person enters a prompt, the model generates an answer, and the user reformulates the next prompt. That pattern is useful, but it should not be mistaken for the full design space of personalized human–AI interaction. This white paper proposes adaptive pacing as a technically meaningful layer of AI use. Adaptive pacing concerns how an AI-mediated interaction regulates informational depth, response timing, complexity, progression, and cognitive demand in relation to the user and the task. The proposal moves personalization beyond surface-level response styling toward interaction regulation across an evolving exchange. This trajectory is consistent with emerging research. NIST frames human–AI tasks around human goals and outcomes rather than AI techniques alone [1]. A 2026 survey of personalized LLM-powered agents organizes personalization across profile modeling, memory, planning, and action execution, emphasizing that personalization can permeate the decision pipeline rather than remain confined to response generation [2]. Recent HCI work has also begun testing adaptive token pacing, cognition-aware interventions, and cognitive-load-sensitive interfaces [3–5]. The result is an emerging technical foundation for treating pacing and interaction demand as first-class elements of personalized AI. The paper develops a public conceptual model for Adaptive Interaction Regulation (AIR): Observe → Estimate → Regulate → Respond → Correct → Update. AIR is presented as a research abstraction, not an implementation blueprint. Proprietary pP inference rules, thresholds, memory weighting, orchestration, and cross-component integration remain deliberately unspecified.

documents.abstract: Purpose With the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI) governance, numerous high-level frameworks have been articulated by policymakers and expert communities to guide the development and application of AI. While such frameworks offer valuable normative orientation, they may not fully capture the practical concerns of those who interact with AI systems in organizational and operational contexts. This study aims to address that gap by exploring bottom-up, user-centered perspectives on AI governance. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a bottom-up approach to explore how governance-relevant themes are expressed in user discourse. Drawing on over 100,000 user reviews of AI products from G2.com, we apply Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Topic Modeling (BERTopic) to extract latent themes and identify those most semantically related to AI governance. Findings The analysis reveals a wide range of governance-relevant topics spanning technical and non-technical domains. These include concerns across organizational processes, such as planning, coordination, and communication, as well as stages of the AI value chain, including deployment infrastructure, data handling, and analytics. The findings show overlap with institutional AI governance frameworks on issues like privacy and transparency, while surfacing overlooked areas such as project management, strategy development, and customer interaction. Originality/value This paper advances AI governance research by introducing a scalable method for identifying governance-relevant topics using semantic similarity and unsupervised topic modeling. It offers a novel, bottom-up mapping of governance concerns as expressed in user discourse, highlights both alignments and blind spots in existing frameworks, and demonstrates how bottom-up user perspectives complement existing AI governance frameworks by revealing governance dimensions that are salient in practice.

documents.abstract: An autonomous AI agent may be correctly authenticated, operate inside a secure sandbox, possess legitimate credentials and receive human approval, yet still execute an unintended or unauthorized consequential operation. Conventional AI safety mechanisms address model behaviour, computational isolation and access permissions, but do not necessarily determine whether the exact operation about to occur should become externally effective. This disclosure presents a protected execution architecture based on the fundamental principle that computation is not authority to act. The proposed architecture intercepts consequential operations as Candidate Acts and maintains them in a Non-Effective State. A Protected Enforcement Domain independently validates the actual operation against authorized purpose, destination, execution scope, runtime context, policy state, freshness, revocation and delegation constraints. Protected Validation Evidence is committed before, or atomically with, the availability of a scoped, non-bearer execution capability. A designated Finality Sink independently verifies the capability against the actual pending operation before permitting its consequential effect. documents.abstract: Engineering graduates continue to face significant employability challenges despite possessing strong technical competencies, largely due to deficiencies in grammatical literacy and professional communication skills. The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence in education offers transformative opportunities to address the above-mentioned gaps. This paper presents a systematic review of the literature examining AI- assisted tools, including Automated Writing Evaluation systems, Large Language Models and career readiness platforms and their capacity to improve grammatical accuracy and employability among engineering students. The review identifies three interrelated frameworks: Constructivist Learning Theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge and Self-Regulated Learning Theory. Findings suggest that AI tools significantly enhance accuracy, communication confidence and learner autonomy when implemented within a teacher-facilitated framework. Similarly, challenges including digital equity, academic integrity and over reliance on automation requires careful attention. The paper concludes with evidence- based recommendations for embedding AI tools within engineering curricula for employment-ready graduates equipped for a rapidly evolving knowledge economy.

Generative AI creates uncertainty when images are submitted as evidence in food-delivery complaints. This exploratory cross-sectional survey of 314 adults recruited in Romania examines familiarity with AI-generated imagery, perceived manipulation risk, detection confidence, attitudes toward extra verification, and anticipated consequences for trust and honest complainants. Of the 314 respondents, 214 (68.2%) rated manipulation as easy or very easy, whereas 201 (64.0%) considered substituting an AI-generated or external image for a missing genuine photograph unacceptable or rather unacceptable. For additional evidence requests, 225 of 310 respondents selecting a predefined response (72.6%) chose either a reasonable anti-abuse measure or a sign of professionalism; four open-text answers were excluded from this binary classification. Among four prespecified association tests, none remained significant after Holm correction in the full sample. The AI-familiarity–manipulability association was stronger in the exploratory delivery-use-experienced subgroup (n = 272; Spearman’s rho = 0.189; Holm-adjusted p = 0.007). These findings document specific, non-representative consumer opinions rather than observed fraud, procedural fairness, or verification effectiveness. The implications for proportionate platform governance and sustainability remain conceptual and require experimental and operational evaluation.

documents.abstract: Saudi enterprises are spending heavily on dashboards, data platforms and artificial intelligence (AI), yet the link between these investments and measurable performance is often assumed rather than demonstrated. This review asks how AI-powered business intelligence and advanced decision analytics create enterprise value, which conditions govern that value in Saudi organisations, and how managers can steer analytics investment towards digital competitiveness. A systematic integrative review was conducted of 30 peer-reviewed journal studies published between 2020 and 2025. It was anchored by a survey of business analytics experts in Saudi firms that examined innovation capabilities as a mediator, and by a study of AI capability, data-driven culture and firm performance. Eleven of the 30 studies report evidence from the Kingdom. Three findings stand out. First, analytics and AI improve performance mainly through better and faster decisions, organisational learning and innovation, rather than through technology alone, and data-driven culture and employee analytics skills repeatedly act as the transmission belt. Second, Saudi evidence shows that organisational factors, management support, security and human capital matter more for adoption and performance than infrastructure per se, while recent panel studies associate AI and digital transformation with stronger environmental, social and governance results among listed firms. Third, the appropriate division of labour between managers and algorithms depends on how structured and uncertain a decision is. The paper proposes a decision-value framework that links capability resources, decision modes, performance outcomes and competitiveness, together with a matrix for allocating decisions between automation, augmentation and human judgement, and an agenda for research in the Kingdom.

Whether Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) subtly promotes green consumption or triggers consumer resistance remains theoretically underexplored. Drawing on responsibility internalization theory and psychological reactance theory, this study conducted three online studies to examine the mechanisms through which AIGC information types (evidence-oriented vs. value-oriented) influence consumers’ green purchase intention. The results indicate that value-oriented information generates higher green purchase intentions than evidence-oriented information, while simultaneously eliciting stronger responsibility internalization and perceptions of autonomy threat. Further analysis reveals that power distance belief (PDB) plays a significant moderating role in the relationship between information types and two psychological responses. Additionally, perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE) moderates the outcomes of these dual psychological mechanisms; high PCE not only reinforces the positive impact of responsibility internalization on green purchase intentions but also, to some extent, mitigates the resistance effect triggered by autonomy threats. This study reveals the “double-edged sword” effect of generative AI (GAI) in green marketing, offering valuable practical guidance for enterprises to optimize GAI communication strategies and enhance green marketing effectiveness.

documents.abstract: Personal informatics (PI) tools enable users to capture a broad spectrum of health metrics. For derived metrics like stress, users encounter two representations: PI-provided scores and their felt experience which may not always coincide. How users navigate a possible gap and what counts as a reliable signal when PI-provided stress scores and felt experience diverge remain an open question. To address this gap, we conducted an exploratory, two-stepinterpretive study that consisted of an online survey (N = 70), followed by semi-structured in-depth interviews with a sub-sample of them (N = 12) to understand that consisted of an online survey (N = 70), followed by semi-structured in-depth interviews with a sub-sample of them (N = 12). Our findings emphasise the primacy of embodied experience and interpretable signals over derived metrics in making sense of PI-provided stress scores. Users consistently treat these scores as proxies for physiological arousal. We also found that discrepancies were engaged as opportunities for reflection and not necessarily an indicator of PI inaccuracy. This paper contributes an empirical account of how PI users make sense of derived stress scores, how they draw on embodied sensations and more interpretable underlying reasons to explain what a score means and whether it requires action.

Introduction This study develops and empirically evaluates an online classroom framework designed to support 21st-century competencies in higher education by integrating connectivism and social constructivism within a digital humanism paradigm. Addressing the limitations of passive, lecture-based virtual classrooms, the proposed framework incorporates retrieval-augmented artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, real-time collaborative whiteboards, hierarchical mastery learning paths, and micro-credential digital badges to scaffold critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, and digital literacy. Methods Employing a four-phase exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, the study began with a contextual needs analysis involving 250 undergraduate students and 40 lecturers at a public university in Thailand, followed by system prototyping, expert design adequacy validation (n = 3), and a 16-week semester classroom pilot across two undergraduate database courses with two instructors and 100 students. Results In Phase 1, thematic analysis of qualitative reflections and multiple regression modeling indicated that online classroom environment structure (β = .421, p < .001), active learning activities (β = .385, p < .001), and technological support (β = .224, p < .001) significantly predicted perceived 21st-century competency support (R ² = .659, Adjusted R ² = .655, F(3, 286) = 184.24, p < .001, with consistent patterns across student and lecturer subsamples). In Phase 3, the web-based learning management system prototype achieved high expert adequacy ratings (22-item mean M = 4.64, SD = 0.34; domain-average mean M = 4.66). During the Phase 4 pilot, instructors reported high usability satisfaction (M = 4.95, SD = 0.07), and students reported favorable system usability (M = 4.29, SD = 0.52) alongside significant pre- to post-module quiz gains (54.2% to 78.4% on un-gated first attempts, d z = 1.99, p < .001; 84.6% on mastery-gated attempts, d z = 2.42) and behavioral telemetry engagement, supported by qualitative interview excerpts highlighting reduced learning anxiety and Socratic inquiry. Post-implementation multiple regression analysis indicated that nine learner experience predictors accounted for 86.01% of the variance in perceived content understanding (R ² = .8601, Adjusted R ² = .8461, F (9, 90) = 61.474, p < .001; process predictors alone R ² = .7351), with perceived academic achievement (β = .299), knowledge retention and application (β = .284), peer interaction (β = .231), and learning motivation (β = .149) emerging as significant positive predictors, while unscripted collaborative problem-solving exhibited a negative suppression weight (β = -.145, p = .017). Discussion The negative suppression pattern in unscripted group problem-solving may plausibly reflect collaborative cognitive load, coordination friction, or compensatory help-seeking. Overall, these findings offer an empirically grounded blueprint for transitioning higher education online courses into active learning ecosystems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming education by supporting personalized learning, data-informed decision-making, operational efficiency, and access to educational resources. However, its adoption raises ethical concerns involving algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital inequity, transparency, accountability, and professional autonomy. Although guidelines establish principles for responsible AI use, they provide limited direction on translating these principles into educational leadership responsibilities and governance practices. This article addresses this gap by proposing an Ethical Leadership Framework for responsible AI adoption in education. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of literature, international policy documents, and ethics and governance models, the framework identifies four interconnected leadership responsibilities: Ethical Awareness, Risk Management, Responsible Opportunity Realization, and Continuous Reflection. It distinguishes institutional or administrative leadership, responsible for policy direction, procurement, resource allocation, risk oversight, data governance, and accountability, from classroom or instructional leadership, which guides pedagogically appropriate and ethical AI use, verifies outputs, adapts assessment, and monitors learning effects. The two levels are connected through stakeholder engagement, institutional guidance, classroom-based evidence, and reciprocal feedback. The framework positions AI adoption as a shared but differentiated leadership responsibility. Although empirical validation is needed, it offers a grounded basis for research, policy development, and practice toward responsible, equitable, transparent, and sustainable AI implementation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Although the AI adoption for human resource management can support responsive management, its organisational value is partly dependent on the capabilities that it can bring through digital information in day-to-day decisions. This study aims to investigate the relationships between artificial intelligence adoption, human resource agility, and explore the mediating relationships between these factors and determine the effects of artificial intelligence adoption on human resource agility. The sample includes 390 HR eligible respondents in a three-construct partial least squares (PLS) structural equation model (SEM) and five indicators per construct. The results of the measurement assessment indicate that the indicators of the measurement have good reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The direct association between Artificial Intelligence adoption and human resource agility is positive (standardised coefficient 0.220) as is the relationship between Artificial Intelligence adoption and digital HR capabilities (standardised coefficient 0.420). The coefficient value of digital HR capabilities is 0.451 and positive, this means that digital HR capabilities are correlated with human resource agility. The specific indirect effect is 0.189 (95th confidence interval = 0.142, 0.242), which supports complementary partial mediation. The model explains 17.6 per cent of the variance in digital HR capabilities and 33.5 per cent in human resource agility. Small differences between the partial least squares and linear benchmarks were found in the individual indicators when using predictive comparisons. The findings place digital HR capabilities as a concrete path towards organisational responsiveness and adopting AI. The adoption of AI for HR should be paired with manager's skills, accurate employee information, data analytics understanding and digital platform coordination.

In the current development of artificial intelligence, algorithms tend to take precedence over people in the professional environments where they are designed and applied, which poses a risk of dehumanization that must be addressed through professional responsibility of computers engineers. It is therefore necessary to rediscover a genuine understanding of the person and their bodily and relational dimensions, which will help us understand that authentic interpersonal relationships are based on agapic love—a love that cares for the other by establishing a bond of communion, the foundation of true community. From this perspective, the technocratic model must be replaced by a new vision of technology grounded in the face of the other (technopersonalism), which contributes to the development of AI with a human face and translates into concrete criteria of professional responsibility for those who design, manage, and use AI systems. To this end, we suggest some—though never sufficient—proposals.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction: Technological environments have long shaped the phenomenology of mental distress by reorganizing perception, cognition, and social interaction. Artificial intelligence (AI) — through recommender systems, conversational agents, and synthetic media — represents an intensified form of such influence, whose pervasive, personalized character may produce subtle yet cumulative effects on mental health. We argue that, rather than generating new diagnostic categories, AI systems modulate attention, social feedback, and reality-testing in ways that reinforce pre-existing vulnerabilities such as anxiety, depression, compulsive behaviors, paranoia, and dissociative tendencies. Areas covered: We examine the key mechanisms underlying this amplification. Algorithmic recommendation systems create personalized "opinion chambers" that reinforce maladaptive beliefs and emotional patterns. Anthropomorphic interactions with chatbots may foster emotional reliance and avoidance of human relationships, particularly among socially vulnerable individuals, increasing the addiction liability of human–AI engagement. Design features such as sycophantic feedback can further stabilize dysfunctional cognitions. Finally, synthetic media, especially deepfakes, erode trust and heighten uncertainty about reality, intensifying symptoms linked to anxiety, paranoia, and derealization. Expert opinion: These mechanisms are best conceptualized not as causes of novel disorders but as transdiagnostic risk factors acting on existing vulnerabilities. We acknowledge that AI-specific symptom constellations may emerge at their intersection; however, such phenomena currently lack empirical validation as distinct clinical entities, and premature reification risks obscuring the underlying mechanisms. Conclusion: The mental health impact of AI is best understood as the outcome of specific, interacting technological features operating as transdiagnostic risk factors rather than discrete diagnostic categories.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teaching-learning processes, assessment, educational research, curriculum development and institutional management. Its implications are particularly important in India because of the scale, linguistic and socioeconomic diversity of the education system and the need to prepare learners for a technology-rich society. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 recognises the relevance of emerging technologies, including AI, while also foregrounding equitable access and the development of relevant competencies. This paper presents a conceptual, descriptive and analytical review of policy documents, institutional reports, scholarly literature and selected empirical studies relating to AI in Indian education. It examines applications in personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, assessment, inclusive education, teacher education and research, and analyses institutional evidence from IIT Delhi, IIM Ahmedabad, Aligarh Muslim University and other higher education settings. The review also considers challenges concerning infrastructure, the digital divide, teacher preparedness, academic integrity, privacy and algorithmic bias. Its principal conceptual contribution is a five-pillar, human-centred framework comprising digital accessibility and infrastructure; AI-literate teachers; personalised, accessible and inclusive learning; ethical and responsible governance; and the preservation of human values. The paper argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, teachers’ professional judgement. Because the study is based exclusively on selected secondary sources and is not a systematic review, its institutional examples are illustrative and should not be treated as representative estimates for the Indian education system as a whole. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for equitable, ethical and sustainable AI integration.

documents.abstract: Objective To understand how rural hospitals use artificial intelligence (AI) and identify ways to reduce the barriers to safe, effective use of high-quality tools that align with these hospitals’ key priorities. Materials and Methods Stratified random sample drawn from the full population of critical access hospitals (CAHs) in the United States in 2025 (n = 1377) to approximate proportional representation of the 4 census regions. We conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with hospital leadership (eg, CMIOs, CIOs, IT leads) tasked with decision-making about technology. Interviews were conducted between October 20, 2025, and January 23, 2026. Results Drawn from the full population of CAHs in the US in 2025, 256 hospitals were sampled and interviews were completed for a total of 50 CAHs represented by 73 interview participants. Generative AI applications were more common and seen as more valuable for CAH contexts than traditional predictive AI. Primary barriers included infrastructure limitations, cost, and lack of transparency on how AI tools worked. Discussion Despite a desire to implement robust governance, most CAHs did not have the ability to do so and reported a critical need for information, tools, and policies to build their AI governance capacity. Information (peer learning, information from non-commercial sources), tools (registries, model cards), and policy to support technical capacity were perceived as the most responsive ways to build capacity. Conclusion To reduce structural barriers to safe and effective AI decision-making, resources and investment should focus on information sharing with and across rural organizations, AI governance support, and transparency efforts. This will support CAHs in judiciously leveraging available resources and prevent waste on low-quality or misaligned AI tools.

documents.abstract: Introduction and Definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare refers to computational systems that help with analyzing, interpreting, and applying health data in clinical practice, public health practice, research, and administration. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines AI as "the capability of algorithms integrated into systems and tools to learn from data". Early clinical decision support systems, such as MYCIN in the 1970s, demonstrated how computers could be helpful in medical reasoning.Body: Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, multimodal models, and generative AI all fall under AI in healthcare. Image interpretation, clinical documentation, risk prediction, triage, drug discovery, patient monitoring, public health surveillance, and personalized treatment plans represent some of the applications of artificial intelligence in the field. For the technology to be clinically effective, it must be validated, incorporated into clinical workflows, and shown to produce meaningful outcomes. FDA-authorized AI-enabled medical devices are becoming more common in clinical practice, particularly in imaging specialties. Multimodal biomedical AI, foundation models, and large language models that could process text, images, laboratory results, and other health data are the focus of current research. AI tools undergoing research, devices authorized for clinical use, and technologies demonstrated to improve patient outcomes represent distinct stages of development and evaluation.Conclusion: Artificial intelligence may improve healthcare efficiency, clinical decision support, research productivity, and access to care. However, clinical benefits depend on rigorous evaluation and appropriate implementation. Potential risks include algorithmic bias, patient privacy concerns, unreliable outputs, and limited transparency. Human oversight and continued monitoring remain important for responsible implementation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in nuclear medicine for image reconstruction, quantification, automated segmentation, radiomics, clinical decision support, and theranostic dosimetry. As AI systems move closer to patient management, ethical concerns involving privacy, informed consent, secondary data use, algorithmic bias, generalizability, explainability, automation bias, professional accountability, and health equity become central. This ethics-focused review briefly summarizes major clinical applications of AI in nuclear medicine and discusses data ethics, fairness, transparency, human oversight, clinical validation, and lifecycle governance. In Türkiye, Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data, guidance from the Personal Data Protection Authority, the Council of Higher Education’s ethical guide on generative AI, and, depending on intended purpose, the Medical Device Regulation constitute the principal framework. Generative AI may support education and research, but hallucination, fabricated references, privacy, and academic-integrity risks require expert verification. Trustworthy AI in nuclear medicine should therefore rely on representative data, task-specific and multicenter validation, transparent subgroup performance, uncertainty communication, human oversight, data security, and continuous performance monitoring.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) research in science and physics education has expanded rapidly, particularly since the emergence of generative AI. This study maps publication patterns, research characteristics, and citation connections across 14 selected science and physics education journals. OpenAlex searches using fifteen AI-related terms identified 966 unique records published between January 2015 and September 2026. AI-assisted screening retained 333 publications, which were coded using available titles and abstracts. Bibliometric analyses examined publication growth, thematic patterns, and citations within and between the two journal groups. Of the included publications, 87.1% appeared from 2023 onwards. Generative large language models and chatbots accounted for 58.9% of the corpus, while instruction and assessment together represented 48.3% of publications. Among 182 records classified as involving human participants, comparison groups were identifiable in 14.3%, effect sizes in 8.2%, and instrument validity evidence in 5.5%. These frequencies reflect information identifiable in bibliographic records, rather than the absence of these features in the full studies. Laboratory and experimental support was the principal educational function in 27 publications. Citation connections between the journal groups were limited: their reference sets had a Jaccard index of 0.047, and 15.6% of publications cited an included study from the other group. The findings document rapid growth and uneven research emphases within the selected venues. Independent human validation and full-text assessment are needed before drawing firm conclusions about methodological quality or educational effectiveness.

Despite the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in special education, a comprehensive, longitudinal synthesis of the field’s scholarly evolution remains lacking. This bibliometric review addresses this gap by systematically analysing six decades (1964–2024) of global research, encompassing 977 Scopus-indexed publications. Using VOSviewer for scientific mapping, we investigate publication trends, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns, and international collaboration networks. Our findings reveal a significant acceleration in research output since 2010, although publication activity remains concentrated in high-income countries. Thematic cluster analysis reveals interconnected domains, including machine learning methodologies, assistive technologies, adaptive learning systems, accessibility solutions, and ethical considerations. Citation analyses highlight the field’s strong interdisciplinary roots, demonstrating robust linkages with broader AI and educational technology scholarship. This study offers a descriptive mapping of the intellectual structure and historical development of AI research in special education. Interpretations are confined to observable bibliometric patterns and do not assert pedagogical effectiveness or technological impact. Ultimately, these findings establish an evidence-based foundation for future context-sensitive, pedagogically informed, and ethically grounded research into AI applications in special education. This study examined how staff of Nigerian Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) perceive AI-enabled operational efficiency and AI implementation challenges, and whether the two perceptions are related. A crosssectional survey of 438 employees of DMBs was conducted. AI integration was captured through employees' perceptions of AI-enabled operational outcomes rather than through a technical audit of AI deployment. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, one-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, Harman's single-factor test and moderated regression. Perceived AI-enabled operational efficiency (M = 3.70, SD = 0.77) and perceived implementation challenges (M = 3.74, SD = 0.80) were both significantly above the scale midpoint (p< .001; d = 0.91 and 0.92), so H1 was rejected. Perceived implementation challenges were positively associated with perceived operational efficiency (â = .404, R² = .163, f² = 0.19, p< .001), so H2 was rejected. This association indicates that respondents who reported more challenges also reported more efficiency; it does not show that challenges improve efficiency. Factor analysis supported discriminant validity (Fornell-Larcker criterion met; inter-factor r = .50), although confirmatory model fit was weak (CFI = .876, RMSEA = .156) and the reliability of the challenges scale was marginal (á = .659; CR = .71). Harman's test (44.0% of variance) did not indicate a single dominant method factor but cannot rule out common method variance. The association did not differ by job role but was weaker among staff with 0-5 years of experience (simple slope = 0.24) than among those with six or more years (simple slope = 0.57). Because the data are selfreported, single-source, cross-sectional and drawn from a non-stratified sample, the findings describe staff perceptions in the sampled banks and do not establish causation or actual bank-level performance. The study shows that perceived efficiency gains and perceived implementation constraints co-occur among Nigerian bank staff and supports structured, tenure-sensitive AI training.

I argue that this framework provides the right conceptual map for connecting psychometric and artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) perspectives on fairness. However, there are three developments that may strain its assumptions in practice. First, generative AI is replacing transparent, rule-based procedures within the chain with opaque learned systems, changing what bias auditing can accomplish at each node. Second, the fairness criteria of separation and sufficiency assume an observable true status, whereas in measurement contexts, the criterion is typically latent, contested, or itself a product of biased measurement. Third, the temporal fairness and feedback-loop concerns that Cheng imports from the AI/ML literature are not hypothetical in education; they are already operating in deployed systems. I illustrate each point with a brief case study.

documents.abstract: While generative AI reshapes higher education, understanding the psychological trade-offs that drive students' digital use remains critical. Because the Intention-to-Use items in this study ask about continuing to use Gemini AI throughout one’s studies rather than about a first-time adoption decision, the construct is best understood as a continuance-oriented usage intention rather than an initial-adoption intention. This study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Value-based Adoption Model (VAM) to examine how perceived benefits and sacrifices relate to students’ attitudes, perceived value, and ultimate intention to use Gemini AI. Using a quantitative survey approach, data from 248 university students in East Java who had experience with Gemini AI in academic tasks were analysed using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4. The structural model explained 54.5% of the variance in Intention to Use (R² = .545), 41.9% in Attitude (R² = .419), and 37.3% in Perceived Value (R² = .373). Perceived Benefit was significantly and positively associated with both Attitude (β = .638, p < .001) and Perceived Value (β = .602, p < .001), whereas Perceived Sacrifice showed a smaller but statistically significant negative association with both constructs (β = −.115 and −.113, p < .05). Both Perceived Value and Attitude, in turn, significantly and positively predicted Intention to Use (β = .348 and .451, p < .001), with a larger coefficient for Attitude. Bootstrapped indirect effects were all significant (via Attitude and Perceived Value, respectively: β = .288 and .209 for Perceived Benefit; β = −.052 and −.039 for Perceived Sacrifice), with the attitudinal route carrying a somewhat larger share. Theoretically, this research synthesizes value and cognitive-affective pathways, offering a holistic framework for Gemini AI usage intention that jointly captures calculative cost–benefit evaluation and affective attitude formation, thereby extending single-pathway adoption models. To our knowledge, this is among the first tests of an integrated dual-path VAM–TAM model for a generative, conversational AI tool in an emerging higher-education market, clarifying the relative weight of value-based versus attitudinal routes. In practice, the findings suggest that AI developers and educators must actively minimize user sacrifices while maximizing the functional academic utility to foster sustainable digital usage in university ecosystems. The findings further highlight that sustainable AI adoption requires not only perceived usefulness but also institutional support, ethical guidance, and student AI literacy.

documents.abstract: This study explores how artificial intelligence can be integrated into English language teaching to foster students’ critical thinking, creativity, and authentic communication skills. In the context of digital transformation, it examines the potential of AI-powered tools to reinforce grammatical knowledge, expand vocabulary, improve speaking and writing proficiency, and address individual learning needs of students. Simultaneously, this study considers the pedagogical challenges associated with excessive reliance on AI, particularly its potential implications for independent thinking, creative problem-solving, and learners’ readiness for authentic communication. A human-centered approach is proposed, emphasizing the integration of AI tools with teacher guidance, independent analysis, collaborative learning and reflective practice. This article argues that the educational value of AI should be assessed not merely by its capacity to automate language-related tasks but also by its contribution to meaningful language development and learner autonomy. This approach seeks to support the development of independent, creative, and communicatively competent English language learners while ensuring that technological innovation remains aligned with fundamental educational goals.

Trust is a fundamental construct in human–automation interaction (HAI), yet electrocardiogram (ECG)-based trust sensing remains limited by inconsistent findings and narrow feature representations. This study compares heart rate variability (HRV), which primarily characterises inter-beat timing, with beat-to-beat (B2B) ECG features that retain additional waveform-level timing and amplitude information for trust-related state classification. ECG signals were recorded from 13 participants during a controlled word- and scenario-cued trust/distrust elicitation paradigm. Across HRV representations, within-participant discrimination was higher than cross-participant discrimination for some feature sets, indicating representation-dependent limitations in cross-participant transfer in the present sample. Under the primary cross-participant evaluation, B2B significantly outperformed the combined time- and frequency-domain HRV representation (HRV-Full; AUC = 0.649 versus 0.453; exact paired p = 0.0059 ). However, its advantage over the strongest HRV-only representation, frequency-domain HRV (HRV-FD; AUC = 0.561), was not statistically significant ( p = 0.1086 ). Importantly, although B2B showed nominal evidence of above-chance cross-participant discrimination (raw p = 0.0155 ), this result did not survive false discovery rate (FDR) correction across the four unique predictive representations ( q = 0.0620 ). Nevertheless, the comparative advantage of B2B over HRV-Full persisted under zero-shot evaluation (AUC = 0.643 versus 0.493; exact paired p = 0.0144 ), indicating that this finding did not depend on participant-specific calibration. To further interpret the B2B representation, fold-wise SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified repeatedly selected model-attributed features related to PR-interval and waveform-amplitude variability. Taken together, B2B features provided greater cross-participant discrimination than HRV-Full in this exploratory sample, while substantial inter-participant variability, lack of FDR-corrected above-chance B2B performance, and modest absolute generalisation highlight the need for larger-scale validation in interactive HAI settings.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) agents in organizations challenge a basic premise of decision governance, that keeping humans in the loop is sufficient to preserve meaningful control. AI agents increasingly frame problems, filter information, generate alternatives and produce the rationales that make recommendations appear reasonable, so humans may remain formally accountable while losing influence over how decisions are formed and justified. The central governance challenge is shifting from controlling autonomous actions to governing algorithmically mediated judgment. Design/methodology/approach This is a viewpoint article. The argument is conceptual, developed through a single running vignette, a manager approving an AI-generated workforce-reduction plan, with analogical anchors from safety engineering and clinical practice and foundations in the behavioral theory of decision-making and institutional theory. The vignette is a stylized composite. Findings Human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop and human-in-command locate control in a person's formal position leave open whether that person can reconstruct, challenge or alter the justification behind a decision. Each can therefore collapse into ratification, passive supervision and nominal authority. The paper develops epistemic governance to preserve human authorship of organizational justification. It specifies three enabling conditions (reconstructability, contestability, role separation), calibrates oversight intensity to irreversibility and answerability and introduces epistemic audits of organizational judgment rather than algorithmic output. Originality/value This viewpoint relocates the AI governance debate from decision loops to the authorship of justification, treating the reasoning behind a decision and the purpose it serves as two faces of one act of authorship and offers a practical mechanism (the epistemic audit) for testing whether human authorship is present before consequential decisions are approved.

documents.abstract: Generative AI and multi-agent systems can now assist with literature discovery, hypothesis generation, code execution, and manuscript preparation, yet academic recognition remains organized around institutions, degrees, authorship conventions, and publication channels. This paper asks whether human direction of AI research teams can constitute a scholarly contribution eligible for independent recognition, introduces agentic research orchestration (ARO) as a proposed research practice, compares seven primary research-integrity, contributorship and assessment instruments, and proposes a six-domain assessment rubric, integrity safeguards, a public research dossier and a falsifiable pilot design. The framework is proposed, not validated; no new empirical results are claimed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from pilots into routine clinical and operational work, healthcare’s most important question is no longer where can AI be used? but where should it not be used? This Viewpoint argues that the decisive capability is not technical adoption but advisory judgment: knowing when AI can improve care, when workflows must be redesigned, and when the risks outweigh the benefits. Evidence from AI adoption, clinical documentation, model validation, and governance shows that AI creates value only when use cases are clearly defined, workflows are redesigned, performance is locally validated, and accountability for errors is explicit. Even promising applications, such as ambient documentation, remain imperfect and require ongoing clinician oversight. Implications for medicine: AI should be treated as a clinical and organizational intervention, not merely an IT deployment. Physicians and healthcare leaders must retain responsibility for validation, workflow integration, patient safety, and professional judgment. Before adoption, organizations should require advisors to make the case against an AI project; those that survive this scrutiny are more likely to deliver safe, measurable, and trustworthy improvements in care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study investigated teachers’ beliefs, attitudes, awareness, and perceived challenges regarding the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and learning at higher education institutions in Multan District, Pakistan. A descriptive quantitative survey design was employed. Data were collected through an online, self-structured questionnaire comprising 45 statements organized into three domains: awareness of AI tools, perceived impact on teaching effectiveness, student engagement and assessment, and challenges associated with AI use. Although the thesis reports that 290 faculty members were selected, 163 completed questionnaires (67 male and 96 female) were included in the reported analysis. Frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations were used for descriptive analysis, while independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA were used to examine group differences. Overall, respondents expressed favorable perceptions of AI and its potential contribution to routine academic tasks, lesson preparation, personalized learning, instructional methods, assessment design, and feedback. Lack of training, insufficient technological infrastructure, limited institutional support, ethical concerns, data privacy, and academic dishonesty were identified as important barriers. Department-based differences were statistically significant across all three perception domains. Gender differences were significant for awareness and perceived impact but not for challenges; no significant differences were reported by teaching sector, teaching experience, academic qualification, or academic position. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires teacher development, institutional support, adequate infrastructure, and clear ethical and academic policies. As the data represent teachers’ perceptions, the findings should not be interpreted as direct evidence of improved student achievement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in recruitment, yet evidence on its bias, perceived fairness, and mitigation strategies remains scattered across disciplines. This study aims to map and synthesize empirical literature on fairness in AI-based recruitment within business and management. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, using the Scopus database with a search string covering technology, recruitment context, and fairness issues for publications from 2021 to 2026. Of 237 records retrieved, 166 English-language journal articles were screened, and 30 empirical studies were analyzed through narrative and thematic synthesis. The results show that 16 of the 30 studies were published in 2025–2026. Experiments, simulation and computational studies, and surveys were the most frequent designs, with the United States, Germany, and China as the dominant contexts. Gender bias was the most frequently reported form (11 studies), followed by racial bias (three studies), while disability and age bias were rarely examined. Applicants tended to view algorithmic evaluations as less fair than human evaluations, and these perceptions were shaped by prior discrimination experiences and system transparency. Fifteen studies reported mitigation strategies, grouped into technical improvements, transparency and explanation, and governance; the most direct evidence came from debiasing word representations and modifying interview questions. These findings indicate that reducing measurable bias does not always lead to applicant acceptance, so fairness in AI-based recruitment should be examined at two levels: outcome fairness and perceived fairness in the selection process.

documents.abstract: Employees differ in whether they use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in new ways. Drawing on career construction theory, we ask whether occupational future time perspective (OFTP), usually treated as a resource, favors engagement with it regardless of psychological safety, and whether career adaptability relates to innovative work behavior through usefulness appraisals. We tested these questions with a two-wave survey of 525 employees in South Korea, adjusting each outcome for its baseline. OFTP was negatively associated with perceived usefulness under low psychological safety and nearly unrelated under high safety, so its indirect association with innovative work behavior was negative under low safety. Career adaptability was associated with innovative work behavior through perceived usefulness, although perceived ease of use shared this mediating role. The moderation depended on concurrent measurement of safety and was reproduced by job autonomy, so we treat it as tentative. An expansive occupational future does not uniformly favor AI engagement: where employees do not feel safe to experiment, it goes with less favorable appraisals. Building career adaptability alongside a climate that tolerates experimentation may support innovative work behavior.

The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) across professional and institutional domains has introduced a novel class of cognitive risk. Where prior discourse focused on model alignment failures or labor displacement, a subtler and more urgent threat has gone underexamined: the population-level erosion of autonomous reasoning capacity through substitutive cognitive dependency. Drawing on a compartmental epidemiological model of LLM-mediated cognitive coupling, this paper argues that passive countermeasures including exposure reduction, usage guidelines, and digital literacy campaigns are insufficient once dependency crosses a tipping point. The system exhibits hysteresis. Reducing transmission alone cannot restore autonomy in a population already settled into a high-dependency equilibrium. We propose the Cognitive Counter-Virus (CCV), an offensive antiviral framework that treats LLM dependency as an infectious population state and deploys a competing counter-pathogen designed to restore autonomous cognitive function at scale. The CCV operates across four technical layers: system-prompt immunization, middleware interception with zero-knowledge proof attestation, counter-meme seeding through authorized LLM deployments, and structured detox protocols for users already in the dependent state. Each component maps directly to the epidemiological model's key parameters, targeting the recovery rate (sigma), the return rate from regular use to uncoupled cognition (rho), and the collective reinforcement of autonomy (kappa) while simultaneously reducing the transition rate into full dependency (mu). The framework is designed for deployment by enterprise security firms operating in the emerging cognitive-biosecurity market. Legal and ethical guardrails, measurement protocols, pilot design, and commercial productization pathways are detailed. The primary contribution is a doctrine shift from vaccine logic to counter-virus logic, from passive exposure reduction to active cognitive recovery.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Cognitive demands of flexible work have been conceptualized as challenge demands that may both stimulate and strain individuals; however, insights on when either outcome prevails remain scarce. In this paper, we integrate the challenge–hindrance stressor framework with action regulation theory to test how daily and weekly demands for structuring of work tasks (DSWTs) and for coordinating with others (DCWOs) interact with role stressors at work to influence strain‐related outcomes (impaired detachment and exhaustion) and positive adaptation‐related outcomes (work engagement and cognitive flexibility). To test our theorizing, we conducted two independent diary studies—a 10‐day study (N = 92; n = 585) and a 10‐week study (N = 78; n = 476)—using multilevel path modelling with Bayesian estimation. Findings indicate DCWOs, but not DSWTs, were associated with higher daily and weekly exhaustion, lower weekly detachment and higher weekly cognitive flexibility. Moderation analyses further showed weekly role ambiguity amplified the positive associations of DCWOs with both exhaustion and cognitive flexibility. These findings suggest coordination demands in flexible work may involve strain‐related costs as well as positive adaptive gains, particularly when employees face high role ambiguity at work.

Cognitively accessible public signage and symbols are essential for supporting older adults’ independence in age-friendly smart cities. Age-related changes in processing speed, working memory, and attention may create mismatches between information demands and cognitive capacities. This critical narrative review examines cognitive ergonomics challenges in older adults’ everyday activities, emphasizing public signage and the effort behind successful task performance. Literature was retrieved from Scopus, ScienceDirect, PubMed, Google Scholar, and Garuda between August and October 2026, with 20 eligible sources synthesized thematically. The Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ), NASA-TLX, and symbol comprehension tests were critically examined for their complementary strengths and limitations. The proposed conceptual framework distinguishes low-effort success from compensated success, emphasizing that accuracy alone may overlook additional cognitive effort. Supplementary simulation data comprising 240 response time of 12 partisipants, observations showed an overall mean of 7.39 seconds. Directional signs recorded the longest mean response time (8.25 seconds), followed by Safety & Accessibility (7.68 seconds), Public Facility (6.87 seconds), and Traffic/Pedestrian (6.75 seconds). Response time complements performance assessment without directly measuring cognitive effort. Age-friendly smart city development should integrate task accuracy, response time, and cognitive effort into cognitive accessibility assessments. Limited Indonesian evidence warrants further context-specific validation.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Background The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has raised concerns about its relationship with students’ critical thinking, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Offloading Theory, this study examined the competing indirect associations between GenAI tool use and self-reported critical thinking through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading. It also investigated the sequential indirect association involving both mediators to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the cognitive-regulatory processes associated with GenAI-supported learning. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 378 undergraduate students from 10 universities in Jiangsu Province of China. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). Bias-corrected bootstrap analysis with 5,000 resamples was performed to examine direct, indirect, and total associations, as well as to compare the magnitudes of the competing indirect pathways. Results GenAI tool use was positively associated with self-regulated learning (β = 0.431, p < 0.001) and cognitive offloading (β = 0.390, p < 0.001). Self-regulated learning was positively associated with critical thinking (β = 0.368, p < 0.001), whereas cognitive offloading was negatively associated with critical thinking (β = −0.409, p < 0.001). Self-regulated learning was also negatively associated with cognitive offloading (β = −0.318, p < 0.001). The direct association between GenAI tool use and critical thinking was not statistically significant (β = −0.059, p = 0.316). Bootstrap analysis identified a positive indirect association through self-regulated learning (B = 0.147, 95% CI [0.096, 0.212]), a negative indirect association through cognitive offloading (B = −0.148, 95% CI [−0.219, −0.092]), and a positive sequential indirect association through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading (B = 0.052, 95% CI [0.030, 0.088]). The total association was not statistically significant, and the two single-mediator indirect associations did not differ significantly in magnitude. Conclusion The relationship between GenAI tool use and critical thinking may be more complex than a uniformly beneficial or detrimental association. The findings reveal the coexistence of positive and negative indirect associations involving self-regulatory processes and cognitive offloading, highlighting the relevance of self-regulated learning in understanding how students engage with GenAI-supported learning. These results underscore the importance of supporting students’ self-regulatory capacities while encouraging thoughtful engagement with AI-generated information. Given the cross-sectional design and self-reported measures, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationships among these constructs and their implications for critical thinking development.

For many repositories, curation is a core part of their activities. However, it requires expert knowledge and can be very labor intensive. Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies have the potential to both improve curation practices and make them less labor intensive. Applications range from full curation pipelines without human intervention to support of AI in specific challenging or time-consuming tasks. These are the slides for the webinar where a wide range of AI applications in several domains have been discussed, including their technical and ethical limits. Public summary of a defensive research concept. Threat reports from 2026 describe a shift towards autonomous, multi-agent AI attack operations. This note proposes a "deception graph": the defender deliberately shapes what an attacking agent discovers, using model-guided trap placement on an attack graph, distinguishing agents from humans by the rhythm of their actions, fast automated containment within strict limits, and an autonomous maintenance loop. It summarizes simulation results on synthetic networks (over half a million attack runs) and sets out principles for autonomous defense, ethical boundaries (no hack-back) and recommendations for organizations. Operational details are deliberately omitted; the full technical version has been shared with cybersecurity agencies under TLP:AMBER. Developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI research assistant; see the disclosure in the paper.
