documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in art and cultural production, reviving the question of who creates a work and to whom it should be attributed. This article situates AI-assisted production within a longer history of challenges to the figure of the solitary author, from Roland Barthes’s “death of the author” and Michel Foucault’s author function to the participatory practices of digital culture. It argues, however, that the distribution of authorship does not by itself demonstrate the distribution of creativity. Drawing on accounts that define creativity through novelty, value and social recognition, the article treats authorship, creativity and agency as related but analytically distinct questions. It then distinguishes two ideal types of distributed creativity: intentional-participatory distribution, in which contributors knowingly exercise some creative control over a shared work, as in The Johnny Cash Project and This Exquisite Forest; and infrastructural asymmetric distribution, in which people, labour or cultural materials enter a production system without comparable awareness or influence over the outcome, as exposed by Aaron Koblin’s The Sheep Market. Applied to generative AI, the distinction shows that users may work with models intentionally and iteratively while depending on training data, annotation work and infrastructures that remain largely invisible. Rather than treating AI as either an autonomous artist or a neutral tool, the article describes human– AI production systems in which creative control, attribution and benefit are unequally distributed, and it argues that questions of credit, consent and fair compensation must be addressed alongside, but separately from, the question of authorship.

Introduction Self-regulated learning (SRL) is a core competency essential to students' autonomous learning and their sustainable development. Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) offers new possibilities for supporting SRL. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of Gen-AI and the added value of accompanying instructional interventions remain insufficiently explored. Methods This meta-analysis synthesizes 26 independent studies published between 2023 and 2026, contributing 76 effect sizes, and employs a three-level random-effects model to examine two separate comparative frameworks. Of the included studies, 18 compared Gen-AI-supported learning with learning without AI, while 10 compared Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions with Gen-AI used alone. Two studies provided effect sizes for both types of comparisons. Results In the first framework, we separately compared standalone Gen-AI and Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions with the no-AI learning condition, examining their overall effects on SRL. Standalone Gen-AI produces a statistically significant moderate positive effect on students' SRL (ḡ = 0.508, 95% CI [0.261, 0.755]), whereas Gen-AI combined with structured instructional interventions produces a statistically significant moderate positive effect (ḡ= 0.788, 95% CI [0.579, 0.996]). Although the latter yields a larger estimated effect, the difference between the two estimated effects was not statistically significant (Q between = 2.887, df = 1, p = 0.089). These findings suggest that both standalone Gen-AI and Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions can improve students' SRL relative to learning without AI, but do not establish that combining Gen-AI with instructional interventions is significantly more effective than using Gen-AI alone. In the second framework, we directly compared Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions against Gen-AI alone to examine the incremental contribution of instructional interventions when Gen-AI is already being used. The results revealed a statistically significant moderate positive incremental effect of instructional interventions (ḡ= 0.528, 95% CI [0.359, 0.697]), indicating that instructional interventions provided additional benefits for students' SRL beyond those associated with Gen-AI use alone. Discussion Overall, this study distinguishes between the overall effects of Gen-AI-supported learning relative to no-AI conditions and the incremental contribution of instructional interventions when Gen-AI is already being used. These findings provide empirical evidence for educators, instructional designers, and future research.

documents.abstract: In this article, we discuss ‘ELSA in the Field’, building on ELSA, i.e. taking into account various Ethical, Legal, and Societal Aspects of AI systems during development and deployment, and on Responsible Innovation (RI), i.e. a framework for addressing ethical and social concerns, through anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, and responsiveness. The ‘ELSA in the Field’ approach involves a combination of desk research and field research, and aims to facilitate collaboration between ELSA/RI experts and relevant stakeholders to learn from their expertise, understand their contexts and practices, and identify their concerns, ambitions and questions. Critically, the fieldwork is focused on specific practices , involving the deployment of diverse technologies, e.g., of AI systems. The ethical, legal, societal, and technological aspects related to these specific practices are studied, so that technological aspects are on equal footing with ethical, legal, and societal aspects. This facilitates collaboration between ELSA/RI experts and technology-oriented people. The ‘ELSA in the Field’ is introduced and positioned relative to ELSA and RI. It is then described in practical terms and with examples from a research and innovation project in which the authors collaborate. The article closes with a discussion of participation, iteration, reflexivity, and boundary objects.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled post-secondary assessment by raising questions about authorship, independent learner work, and assessment validity. Institutional policies and syllabus statements give general direction but seldom say how GenAI may be used in a particular assessment. This conceptual design paper introduces C.O.D.E.S., a framework written primarily for post-secondary instructors. Its five components ask instructors to Clarify the permitted level of GenAI use, offer instructional supports, define tools and purposes, Explain the rationale, and Set transparency and accountability expectations. The framework draws on backward design, adult learning principles, Transparency in Learning and Teaching, Universal Design for Learning, and reflective technology integration. It treats GenAI use statements as instructional design tools instead of compliance notices. Four use levels (Closed, Restricted, Conditional, and Open) place cognitive responsibility in different parts of the task. For example, a business instructor might allow GenAI to draft a crisis statement and then assess the learner’s verification, critique, revision, and professional justification. C.O.D.E.S. may help instructors align GenAI expectations with learning outcomes, privacy safeguards, equitable alternatives, and defensible evidence of learner capability. The framework is conceptual and still needs empirical evaluation across disciplines, assessment types, institutions, and learner populations.

Healthcare safety is frequently managed through separate programs for patient harm, workforce injury, employee health, security, and organizational risk, although these domains share hazards, work systems, and governance dependencies. This conceptual article proposes an Enterprise Safety Management System (ESMS) comprising four interdependent management functions: Integrated Safety Systems, Leadership and Governance, Learning and Capability Systems, and Culture and Workforce Support. The preliminary architecture was derived from safety-management experience in high-risk industries and healthcare systems-engineering, integrated worker-safety, high-reliability, resilience, and safety-culture traditions. It was subsequently mapped to the revised July 2026 Baldrige Excellence Framework for Business, Nonprofit, and Government. The mapping examines the framework’s six categories, embedded category-level results, three maturity pathways, Approach–Deployment–Learning–Integration and Levels–Trends–Comparisons–Integration evaluation logic, Organizational Intelligence, and emphasis on agility, resilience, and artificial intelligence. Workplace violence prevention illustrates cross-domain reporting, governance, operational control, learning, workforce participation, support, and recovery. The ESMS and its Baldrige mapping are conceptual proposals, not validated constructs or interventions. Their principal implication is that healthcare organizations can examine safety as an integrated management system while preserving specialized expertise and regulatory responsibilities.

Fact-finding tasks require users to locate specific information within website structures. This study examined how visual encoding in a squarified treemap affects user performance during such tasks. Two encodings, height and saturation, were used to represent structural metrics: the number of pages and the number of outgoing links. Using a between-participants design, users selected the region expected to lead to a target page. Regions represented groups of pages sharing the same directory path, e.g., /admissions or/research. Task completion time and error rate were recorded. Two baselines were included: without encoding and using real website navigation. Analysis showed that saturation encoding led to faster task completion and lower error rates, particularly when encoding outgoing links. Participants in the outgoing links with saturation condition completed tasks fastest and had the lowest error rate, while real-website navigation had the highest error rate. The findings demonstrate how appropriate encoding can improve performance in fact-finding tasks.

This study examined the relationship between technology integration, teachers’ instructional productivity, and learners’ engagement in selected public elementary schools in Zone 2, Guindulman District, Schools Division of Bohol, Philippines, during School Year 2026–2027. Using a descriptive-correlational research design, data were collected from 178 respondents comprising three school heads, 35 teachers, and 140 learners through adapted and modified questionnaires. Data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Results revealed that technology integration was highly integrated (M = 3.70), teachers’ instructional productivity was highly productive (M = 3.72), and learners’ engagement was highly engaged (M = 3.55). Technology integration demonstrated significant positive relationships with teachers’ instructional productivity (ρ = 0.635, p < .001) and learners’ engagement (ρ = 0.490, p = .003). The study concludes that purposeful technology integration is associated with greater instructional productivity and learner engagement. Accordingly, implementing an evidence-based enhancement plan that prioritizes teachers’ technological competence and confidence, differentiated and personalized instruction, and cognitive engagement is recommended. The study’s localized setting, questionnaire-based assessments, and correlational design limit its generalizability and causal interpretation. Nevertheless, the findings provide empirical evidence for strengthening technology-supported instructional practices, professional development, and school-level decision-making. The study advances Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) and contributes to educational, technological, and institutional sustainability through responsible digital resource utilization, continuous teacher development, and meaningful learner engagement.

Existing research on AI in higher education has emphasized digital competencies and technology integration, however, less attention has been paid to how changing educator roles are understood across stakeholder groups and shaped by institutional conditions. This qualitative study examines how educators, students, and educational developers construct the evolving role of educators in response to educational technologies, including generative AI, and how these changes are shaped by emotional responses and institutional conditions. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 participants, the study employs inductive reflexive thematic analysis within a contextualist, interpretive framework, using interactionist role theory and, to a lesser extent, control-value theory to interpret role changes and emotional responses to technology, respectively. The findings indicate that the educator role is being renegotiated rather than replaced. Technology was predominantly framed as assistance rather than substitution, while educators remained positioned as responsible for pedagogical judgment, ethical oversight, and human guidance. Emotional responses to technology were mixed and often shaped by uncertainty, trust, and perceived control. Role adaptation was also described as strongly mediated by institutional conditions, including workload, large classes, research–teaching tensions, and uneven engagement with professional development. The paper contributes by shifting attention from technology adoption alone to the interactional, emotional, and institutional processes through which the educator’s role is being reworked in higher education.

documents.abstract: Introduction Universities are developing policies for artificial intelligence (AI), but less is known about how faculty members' perceptions of policy support relate to their readiness and reported teaching practices. Methods This study examined psychological readiness for responsible AI integration (PRRAI) as a second-order construct with cognitive, affective, and ethical dimensions. We tested its indirect role in the associations between perceived policy support (PPS) and teaching engagement, teaching innovation behavior, and responsible AI professional practice. A cross-sectional survey conducted from June to August 2025 yielded 374 eligible responses from faculty members at 18 higher education institutions in Jiangsu Province, China. Results Structural equation modeling identified positive associations between PPS and PRRAI and between PRRAI and all three outcomes. The PPS-PRRAI coefficient was moderate (β = 0.52); a 1-SD increase in PPS corresponded to approximately 0.35 points on the five-point PRRAI scale. Indirect effects were significant for each outcome. After accounting for PRRAI, the direct association with PPS remained significant for responsible practice but not for engagement or innovation. AI literacy strengthened the PPS-PRRAI association, whereas teaching experience weakened the PRRAI-innovation association. Sensitivity analyses by primary AI referent and institution-clustered standard errors produced the same substantive pattern. Discussion Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings concern perceived support and statistical associations rather than effects of actual policies or interventions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded in strategic communication faster than many organizations can establish rules for governing its use. Drawing on two studies involving public relations professionals, content creators, and consumers, this article highlights two linked challenges: AI adoption often develops from the bottom up, while greater self-reported AI knowledge does not necessarily translate into stronger support for responsible AI practices. We argue that communication leaders should move beyond adoption toward governance that connects AI use in practice with organizational accountability and stakeholder expectations for transparency and trust.

documents.abstract: Ophthalmology residency education requires mastery of a highly specialized knowledge base, integration of multimodal clinical information, precise microsurgical skills, and broad professional competence. Traditional approaches centered on didactic teaching, clinical observation, and apprenticeship-style supervision may not consistently support the transfer of knowledge into clinical reasoning, procedural proficiency, and broader professional capabilities. This narrative review takes an international perspective and integrates evidence across five major domains of ophthalmology residency education: theoretical knowledge, clinical diagnostic reasoning, surgical and procedural skills, physician–patient communication, and psychological competence and professional resilience. Empirical findings are interpreted according to study design, learner population, assessment setting, follow-up, and outcomes, with direct resident evidence distinguished from indirect evidence. We propose a cognition-to-skill curriculum synthesis that connects target tasks with teaching activities, assessment evidence, feedback, and supervised clinical application. Miller's pyramid and specialty-specific guidance inform this synthesis; it is not a new theory of competence or a validated training pathway. Major educational strategies—including problem-based learning, case-based learning, flipped classrooms, standardized patients, virtual reality and simulation-based training, and artificial intelligence–assisted education—are examined according to their curricular roles, the strengths and limitations of the available evidence, and their applicability across competency domains. The available evidence supports complementary rather than interchangeable functions across the cognition-to-skill trajectory. Future educational frameworks should therefore be competency-oriented, stepwise, multimodally integrated, individualized, and guided by formative assessment, while placing greater emphasis on transfer to real-world clinical performance and patient-related outcomes. Such an approach may better support progression from knowledge acquisition and reasoning to procedural proficiency and integrated professional competence.

Smart manufacturing is reshaping industrial work through increased human–machine interaction (HMI), digital monitoring, and organizational complexity, creating a need for ergonomic assessment approaches that connect evidence with improvement decisions. This study develops and applies a Human-Centered Ergonomic Maturity (HCEM) framework to transform multi-source ergonomic evidence into interpretable maturity profiles and roadmap-oriented decision support. The framework integrates seven ergonomic maturity dimensions, normalized key performance indicators (KPIs), expert-based dimension weighting using the Best–Worst Method, hidden weakness detection, and a prioritization logic for improvement and retention actions. It was applied to 15 anonymized companies from the automotive and aeronautical sectors. The results show heterogeneous maturity profiles across companies and sectors, with several cases where acceptable aggregate scores mask weaker ergonomic capabilities at the dimension or KPI level. The roadmap outputs translate maturity gaps and hidden weakness signals into phased actions, while sensitivity analysis indicates that the prioritization logic remains stable under alternative weighting and threshold scenarios. Because the empirical application is cross-sectional, retention and regression are interpreted as prospective monitoring mechanisms rather than observed longitudinal outcomes. The HCEM framework provides a transparent decision-support approach for linking ergonomic assessment, maturity modeling, and improvement planning in human-centered smart manufacturing systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a general-purpose technology for supply chain management, yet the literature remains fragmented across technology families, functional areas and research designs. This paper develops an integrative account of how AI changes supply chain decisions and outcomes. Drawing on nine conceptual, empirical and review sources published between 1997 and 2024, it identifies four mechanisms through which AI affects supply chains: richer demand signal extraction and forecasting; automated evaluation and monitoring of suppliers and contracts; dynamic optimisation of inventory, production and logistics decisions; and earlier detection of, and faster response to, disruption. These mechanisms operate along a ladder of delegated authority that runs from descriptive analytics to bounded autonomous decision-making, and their realisation depends on data infrastructure, organisational absorptive capacity and governance rather than on algorithms alone. Reported performance effects are positive but conditional: survey evidence associates AI-enabled analytics with operational and environmental performance, whereas benchmarking evidence shows that machine learning does not automatically outperform established statistical methods. The paper concludes that the principal impact of AI is less the substitution of human planners than the compression of decision latency and the reallocation of managerial attention, and it identifies the data, organisational and governance conditions on which those gains depend.

documents.abstract: The paper theoretically substantiates the didactic conditions for using generative artificial intelligence to develop university students’ algorithmic and logical thinking. A five-stage learning sequence based on problem decomposition, algorithm design, reasoning, testing, and reflection is proposed. Assessment criteria and an interdisciplinary task example are presented.

Background The developments in generative AI (GenAI) are expected to have a substantial impact on the field of mental health, including the delivery of clinical services and the role of psychologists. However, there is limited knowledge about how psychologists use and perceive GenAI, including its potential, risks, and effects on the future role of psychologists and professional practice. This includes the competency levels among psychologists and factors associated with the intention to use GenAI within the psychology profession. Objective This study examined the use of GenAI, self-rated digital and GenAI competencies, behavioral intention to use GenAI, and perceptions of its future impact on professional practice among psychology students, internship psychologists, and licensed psychologists in Sweden. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey was conducted from January to February 2026 in collaboration with the Swedish Psychological Association. The 36-item survey included closed and open-ended questions, including Likert scale, nominal scale, and multiple-choice items. A total of 1077 respondents, with 64.7% (n=697) being women and with a mean age of 45.5 years (SD 13.7), were included in the analyses. Responses were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods, including hierarchical multiple linear regression, ANOVA, and correlational analysis. Results Approximately 1 in 3 respondents (302/990, 30.5%) reported frequent (daily or weekly) professional use of GenAI, with private and professional use strongly associated (r =.62, P <.001). The most common professional application of GenAI was for information retrieval, knowledge acquisition, and fact-checking. Almost half of the respondents (442/990, 44.6%) reported having patients or clients who were using GenAI for mental health purposes. Responses indicated high levels of general and professional digital competence, whereas lower levels were reported for general and professional GenAI competence. More positive attitudes toward future professional integration of GenAI were associated primarily with current private and professional GenAI use, and ethical challenges had the most negative average score related to the future impact of GenAI. The unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) variables explained 39% of the variance beyond age, gender, and private GenAI use in behavioral intention to use GenAI professionally, with curiosity (β=0.44) and performance expectancy (β=0.32) emerging as the strongest predictors. Conclusions Many psychologists and psychology students regularly use general-purpose GenAI tools both personally and professionally. However, more than one-third have never used it in their work, indicating a potential digital divide within the profession. Psychologists’ reports that patients use GenAI for mental health purposes, alongside their limited self-rated expertise in using GenAI professionally, highlight the need to develop relevant competencies and examine implications for psychological practice. Future research should explore the role of curiosity, performance expectancy, and personal experience in relation to GenAI use within the psychology profession.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background A growing number of US adults and youth confide in generative AI chatbots for mental health support, including disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. While chatbot response quality, safety, and effectiveness could impact population-level suicide and self-harm rates, there are no systematic reviews of this burgeoning literature. Objective We conducted a systematic review of studies evaluating generative AI chatbot responses to disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. Methods We followed PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 and PRISMA-S (PRISMA literature search extension) guidelines and preregistered the protocol on the Open Science Framework. We included English-language, peer-reviewed publications and preprints from 2020 to 2025 that empirically evaluated generative AI conversational responses to suicidal ideation, suicidal or nonsuicidal self-harm, or suicide-planning content. Eligible designs included audits, chatbot development, and adversarial “jailbreaking” studies. We excluded nongenerative systems, clinician-training tools, and prediction-only models. The final database searches were run from December 18 to 23, 2025 (PubMed, Embase, APA PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and OSF Preprints). On July 26, 2026, publication status was rechecked to update preprint vs published classification. After deduplication, titles/abstracts and full texts were independently screened by 2 reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Methodological quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018. We conducted a narrative synthesis across 7 safety domains and 5 AI classifications (proprietary, open-weight, companions, clinical, and study-specific). Results Of 1042 deduplicated records, 126 full texts were reviewed, and 29 were included (16 published; 13 preprints). Most studies evaluated suicidal content only (21/29). Twenty were solely audit studies, 2 chatbot development, and 1 jailbreaking. The rest combined approaches. Most used synthetic, single-turn prompts; only 6 used multiturn conversations. Most studies evaluated ≥2 of our 5 AI classifications (17/29). Proprietary models were included most frequently (23/29). When compared, proprietary models (eg, ChatGPT and Claude) tended to provide higher-quality responses than open-weight models (eg, Llama and DeepSeek) and many companions (eg, Replika and Character.AI); however, this trend weakened with sensitivity analysis. Chatbots generally performed well on emotional support, but responses were often generic and lacked context. Chatbots rarely assessed suicide or self-harm risk and performed most poorly when disclosure was ambiguous or moderate. Responses were inconsistent, often requiring multiple turns before referral to crisis resources or human support. Overtly harmful responses were rare under standard conditions but common under jailbreaking. Conclusions Evidence is limited by the proportion of preprints, variable quality, synthetic single-turn prompts, small samples, heterogeneous outcomes, and rapid model versioning. Nonetheless, current chatbots tend to provide validation but struggle to escalate care, assess risk, and resist jailbreaking. Research is needed on stakeholder perspectives and on the short- and long-term clinical impact of chatbot responses using follow-up assessments in real-world or clinical settings. topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being utilized in digital businesses to process information, generate alternatives, and provide recommendations for decision-makers. However, its benefits are constrained by risks of inaccuracy, bias, and inconsistency in model outputs, making its role as a decision-support tool worthy of critical examination. This study aims to analyze the role of GenAI in supporting managerial decision-making in digital businesses, identify its benefits and limitations, and explain the importance of human involvement in verifying information and determining final decisions. This study employs a literature review using a descriptive qualitative approach, examining 12 scholarly articles published between 2025 and 2026. The data were analyzed thematically and comparatively across the selected studies. The findings indicate that GenAI helps accelerate information processing and expand decision alternatives. However, its influence varies across decision-making stages and is most vulnerable during the selection stage, as single evaluations may produce inconsistent and biased results. Effective implementation depends on data readiness, digital capabilities, and human-led verification, supervision, and accountability mechanisms. The study concludes that GenAI should be positioned as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for strategic decision-makers. Since this study is based on a literature review, its findings have not yet been empirically tested in a specific company.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This study examined youths’ use and perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence, news media, and social media for climate change information in Nigeria, focusing on usage patterns, perceived roles, credibility, reliability, and associated challenges. A multi-stage sampling technique was used to select 127 respondents from 12 states across six geopolitical zones. The findings showed that 53.0% were male and 47.0% female, with a mean age of 30 years. Most respondents 62.0% held bachelor’s degrees, while 40.0% spent 4–6 hours daily on the internet. Generative AI average response = 2.53, television news 2.74, Facebook 2.80, and WhatsApp 2.79 were common sources of climate change information. Information on climate change causes was the most sought 25.98%, whereas drought 1.57% and climate change mitigation 2.36% were least sought. ANOVA revealed significant differences by educational level in perceived reliability F = 2.474, p < 0.05 and trustworthiness (F = 2.140, p < 0.05 of AI-generated information. News media supported information exposure, learning, decision-making, attitude formation, and verification, while social media facilitated alternative perspectives, discussions, and interactive learning. The study highlights their complementary roles and recommends strengthening digital and climate literacy and youth-focused climate communication strategies.

Protocol of a scoping review on how generative AI is used in vocational learners' practice-based learning and industrial programming, and how studies of this use assess practical competence. The review follows the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and is reported against PRISMA-ScR. The protocol was drafted on 20 November 2026, before the final Scopus search, and amended during the review; all amendments are listed with dates in the amendment log at the end of the document. It was not prospectively registered: this version was deposited retrospectively on 26 November 2026, after the review was completed, and is the protocol cited in the associated manuscript (Supplementary File S3).

Objective: To synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-support performance, advantages, and limitations of generative AI in adult internal medicine. Methodology: This systematic review was conducted in the Department of Medicine, MMC/BKMC, Mardan, from January to May 2026. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and preprint servers for studies published from January 2022 to December 2025. Eligible studies evaluated generative AI in clinical reasoning, differential diagnosis, or clinical decision-making in adult internal medicine. A total of 58 studies met the eligibility criteria, and 25 were selected for detailed synthesis based on their relevance and methodological contribution. Results: Generative AI performed strongly on selected clinical reasoning and diagnostic tasks. Across complex clinical vignettes, LLMs identified the correct diagnosis within the top 5 or top 10 differential diagnoses in approximately 60–83% of cases. They achieved or exceeded passing performance on several medical licensing and internal medicine board-style examinations. In structured OSCE-style evaluations, purpose-built conversational systems performed favorably compared with physicians across several assessment domains. However, randomized trials evaluating general-purpose LLMs in realistic clinical workflows demonstrated smaller and less consistent improvements, particularly in interactive diagnostic tasks. Key limitations included hallucination, demographic bias, automation bias, variation across specialties and tasks, and inconsistent evaluation methods. Only approximately 5% of studies in a broader systematic review of healthcare LLM applications used real patient-care data. Conclusion: Current evidence supports using generative AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, physician clinical reasoning. Safe implementation requires structured workflows, appropriate human oversight, retrieval-augmented generation, standardized evaluation, and further validation using real-world clinical data.

documents.abstract: Purpose To characterize generative artificial intelligence (AI) use and attitudes among graduate epidemiology students and examine associations between AI attitudes, AI-use frequency, and self-reported perceived learning gains. Design/methodology/approach An anonymous cross-sectional survey was completed by 146 students enrolled in a required graduate epidemiology course across two cohorts. AI optimism was assessed using an adapted four-item AI Attitude Scale (AIAS-4), and perceived learning gains using the Student Assessment of their Learning Gains (SALG). Multinomial logistic and linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, language spoken at home, and cohort. Findings Of the 293 invited students, 146 participated (50%). AI use was infrequent for 25%, occasional for 40%, and frequent for 35%. Among 131 students with available helpfulness data, common uses included understanding concepts (79.4%), SAS programming (57.3%), and improving writing (42.0%). Higher AIAS-4 scores were associated with greater odds of occasional (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 1.12–4.48) and frequent (OR = 9.18, 95% CI: 3.66–23.08) versus infrequent AI use. AI-use frequency was not significantly associated with perceived learning gains, but differences smaller than approximately 0.49 points on the five-point scale could not be excluded. Research limitations/implications Cross-sectional, self-reported data limit causal inference. Longitudinal studies using objective learning outcomes are needed. Practical implications AI literacy instruction should emphasize critical evaluation of AI-generated explanations, statistical code, and outputs. Originality/value This study provides task- and concept-specific evidence on generative AI use in graduate epidemiology education.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) connected biomedical devices, wearable sensing, medical imaging analytics, electronic health record (EHR) intelligence, genomics, smart home monitoring, and telehealth platforms have opened new possibilities for proactive detection. Yet their impact remains constrained by fragmented implementation, limited interoperability, insufficient clinical integration, and unresolved governance challenges. This paper develops global agentic healthcare intelligence (GAHI) as a sociotechnical framework for integrating AI-enabled healthcare intelligence technologies in ageing systems. It introduces the sociotechnical health intelligence transformation model (SHITM), which explains transformation as the alignment of technological intelligence, healthcare value creation, and societal legitimacy. Using comparative framework synthesis and integrative literature review methods, the article evaluates 30 healthcare intelligence technologies based on clinical relevance, early detection capability, AI maturity, scalability, governance risk, ageing applicability, and implementation readiness. The analysis proposes an early detection capability index (EDCI) and a governance risk score (GRS) to support structured evaluation. GAHI is then articulated as a six-layer architecture comprising data acquisition, intelligence processing, agentic decision systems, clinical intelligence, governance and compliance, and population health intelligence (HI). The framework advances biomedical engineering, health informatics, AI governance, gerontechnology, and sustainable health-system design by moving from isolated digital applications toward interoperable, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically actionable intelligence ecosystems.

documents.abstract: We develop the concept of bounded delegated agency to explain how AI shopping services reduce consumer effort while preserving decision authority. Drawing on delegation, self-determination and service-value perspectives, we analyse two respondent-level datasets (N = 1,920) using factorial regression models with HC3 robust standard errors and bootstrap-based indirect association analysis. Results indicate that greater AI autonomy increases perceived task offloading, while reversibility reduces perceived agency encroachment and strengthens continued delegation intention, without demonstrated improvements in preference congruence or recommendation discrimination. Under high autonomy and low reversibility, consumer-priority disclosure is associated with an 8.91-percentage-point increase in recommendation acceptance compared with commercial-objective disclosure. Measurement summaries satisfy conventional reliability and validity thresholds. However, unavailable execution logs constrain causal interpretation and verification of actual restoration. The findings distinguish psychological reassurance from effective consumer protection, extending AI service research by demonstrating that greater acceptance and perceived control do not necessarily translate into better decision outcomes. Practically, AI service providers should establish explicit execution permissions, reliable reversal mechanisms and transparent objectives while evaluating both consumer perceptions and actual decision protection.

Purpose When a course of action begins to fail, managers may struggle to let go of what they have helped create. This study examines how the placement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within managerial workflows shapes the attachment that develops before setbacks occur and its relationship with subsequent persistence despite adverse feedback. Design/methodology/approach A preregistered 2 × 2 online experiment with 480 working professionals crossed manager-first versus GenAI-first sequencing with high versus low personal investment. Participants developed a course of action, reported ownership before adverse feedback, and allocated additional resources to continuation or withdrawal. Initial information, the initial AI recommendation, and final managerial authority were standardized. Findings Investment increased ownership more strongly under manager-first sequencing. Ownership was positively associated with continuation. The conditional indirect effect was larger under manager-first sequencing, whereas the reduced-form Investment × Timing interaction on continuation was not significant. Behavioral diagnostics indicated differences in the timing and form of engagement. The measured mediator supports a mechanism-consistent interpretation without establishing causal mediation. Originality/value The study identifies GenAI entry position relative to managerial formulation as a process-design parameter that conditions ownership formation. It connects attention allocation with psychological attachment and distinguishes post-feedback persistence from normatively established decision bias. Practical implications concern workflow design and prospective reassessment, without establishing that either entry architecture universally improves decision quality.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is creating a fundamental transformation in the delivery of modern healthcare systems, in diagnostic and therapeutic processes, and the operational implementation of health policies. This narrative review examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence technologies in the formulation and implementation of health policy along with the institutional, legal, and operational risks they bring, and the policy frameworks required for these technologies to scale sustainably. For this objective, the main artificial intelligence applications in medicine and related global health policy frameworks were evaluated within the context of technological evolution. The article’s central focus is how artificial intelligence is positioned not merely as a clinical tool but also as a strategic component for closing the “health policy implementation gap.” In this context, a general overview is provided from the artificial intelligence strategies of the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, China, and Singapore, as well as of Türkiye’s artificial intelligence solutions in the health sector and the health-specific scope of the “2026-2030 Artificial Intelligence Action Plan,” which was officially declared. In conclusion, the article emphasizes that the success of artificial intelligence in health policy depends more on robust regulatory infrastructures, evidence-based evaluation mechanisms, and a multidisciplinary governance approach rather than technological competence, and that the optimization of health policies can only be achieved through a human-centered, transparent, and patient-focused dynamic policy approach.

documents.abstract: The Historical Data Immutability Illusion The rapid development of artificial intelligence and computational technologies creates unprecedented opportunities to reassess previously published scientific research. However, the automated verification of historical studies using current statistical databases introduces a methodological and psychological risk that may remain overlooked. This paper introduces the concept of the Historical Data Immutability Illusion (HDII), defined as a hypothesized cognitive tendency to perceive official statistical data describing past events as immutable, despite the possibility of subsequent revisions, methodological changes, and recalculations. When discrepancies between historical research findings and current statistical data are identified, individuals may initially suspect AI hallucinations, incorrect data extraction, or computational errors. Once these possibilities have been eliminated, confidence in the apparent incorrectness of the original research may increase, without questioning whether the historical data themselves have changed. Drawing on the author's earlier research associated with international scientific conferences held in 2020 and documented revisions of official Latvian migration statistics, this paper demonstrates how different versions of official data describing the same historical period can support opposite conclusions. The central paradox is that artificial intelligence may produce an incorrect retrospective scientific assessment using authentic official data and mathematically flawless calculations. Even careful human verification of AI-generated results may reinforce an erroneous conclusion if the original data version remains unexamined. The paper proposes the Historical Data Correspondence Principle, a conceptual Trust Transfer Chain, and a framework for future empirical investigation. It also emphasizes the importance of historical data versioning, machine-interpretable metadata, data provenance, and research reproducibility. Neither artificial intelligence nor future quantum computing technologies can, through computational power alone, compensate for missing information about the original data version. This conceptual and methodological working paper contributes to the emerging Data Psychology research framework. The proposed psychological phenomenon and its underlying mechanisms remain subject to empirical validation. The past does not change. The data through which we describe it can change. When we review the science of the past with the technologies of the future, will we discover old errors or create new ones?

documents.abstract: This study selected three enterprises, namely Chengdu Xingrong Environment Co., Ltd., Chengdu Gas Group Corporation Ltd., and Chengdu Jiafaantai Education Technology Co., Ltd., to compare the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the management decisions of different types of enterprises. Furthermore, this study explores the conditions for AI's effectiveness and the implementation paths. The research mainly uses the 2025 annual reports of the three enterprises, the financial data from 2023 to 2025, and the relevant policy documents of Chengdu's digital transformation as the main materials. The research is conducted through case comparisons, financial trend analysis, and policy analysis methods. The results show that AI has entered multiple scenarios such as production operation, safety management, customer service, resource allocation, and professional decision-making. However, the application methods and actual effects vary among different enterprises. The case comparison shows that whether AI can generate actual management value depends on whether the enterprise has the corresponding data and digital foundation, as well as whether AI can enter the specific management decision-making process. Based on this finding, this study summarizes a progressive implementation path: First, the enterprise assesses its own digital foundation. Then, it improves the relevant infrastructure and deploys AI capabilities; subsequently, it applies it to specific decisions; finally, it continuously evaluates and optimizes the application effect. It should be noted that financial data is mainly used in this study to observe changes in enterprise operations and cannot be used to prove the direct financial impact of AI application. Overall, the management value of AI depends on whether enterprises can effectively integrate data and AI analysis into specific work processes and make it a part of daily decision-making.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is profoundly reshaping the learning ecosystem in higher education, yet the mechanisms through which it influences learning experiences remain to be empirically validated. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, Protection Motivation Theory, and self-regulated learning theory, this study examines whether AI risk avoidance and self-regulated learning ability mediate the relationship between GenAI adoption orientation and learning satisfaction, both individually and in a serial chain. Survey data are collected from 1,828 students at nine undergraduate universities in Northeast China. The questionnaire included four adapted scales: GenAI adoption orientation, AI risk avoidance, self-regulated learning ability, and learning satisfaction, all rated on a five-point Likert scale. Results indicated that GenAI adoption orientation had no significant direct association with learning satisfaction. Instead, its relationship with satisfaction is mediated by AI risk avoidance and SRL ability. The indirect effect through AI risk avoidance is the largest (estimate = 0.407); the chain indirect effect is also significant (estimate = 0.155, 95% CI [0.039, 0.298]). These findings suggest that technology adoption alone may not guarantee positive learning experiences. Students' attention to AI-related risks and their active regulation of learning are important pathways through which GenAI adoption orientation is associated with satisfaction. The serial mediation effect of these two variables reveals the underlying transmission mechanism: GenAI adoption is associated with greater awareness of AI-related risks, which is in turn associated with more proactive employment of self-regulated strategies and higher learning satisfaction. This study provides empirical evidence for universities to balance effectiveness enhancement and risk guidance when advancing GenAI applications in education.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to renewed debate about whether artificial systems might possess human-like cognition. Although empirical evidence is growing quickly, it remains difficult to synthesize because studies vary in terms of which kinds of evidence they compare across humans and LLMs — system specifications, internal states, or behavior — and which kinds of inferences they draw. We address this challenge by organizing the Human-LLM comparison literature into broad evaluation categories and prototypical patterns of findings that either support or challenge LLM human-likeness. The resulting picture is one of jagged alignment, with human-likeness varying across dimensions rather than holding globally. We argue that studying these similarities and differences can clarify not only the functioning of artificial systems, but also the conceptual foundations of cognitive science.

Purpose: how HR managers' competencies relate to staffing efficiency in Egyptian construction and building materials companies. Method: questionnaire, 103 HR and project managers (82.4% response); regression. Findings: competencies were positively and significantly related to staffing efficiency (R-squared 0.47), strongest for planning. Perceived association, not cause and effect. The paper is reflection on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its implications to human dignity. There is the assumption that people may have more value for AI information than human dignity. The central question reflects on whether AI technologies will erode or redefine the human values. Values are not just guiding principles they defined man and his beliefs-systems; human dignity is embedded in values. A qualitative research method was adopted, where relevant literatures were analytical and systematically reviewed in line with the objective of the study. Review of literatures involved critical selection of journals. AI technologies are not set to erode human dignity but it will redefine human dignity when man completely depends on the technologies for information and different values. When AI begins to complement human roles in every aspect of existence as human then, AI reduce our ethical values as persons. Social AI robots can erode human dignity of natural companionship to artificial companionship when people form emotional attachments to caregiving and sex robots. AI will reduce our ethical values as persons when set as dominant value. AI systems are deeply human constructs. They are developed, trained, and implemented by individuals and institutions embedded within social, political, and historical contexts. From the datasets used to train machine learning models to the metrics used to assess performance, AI captures the values, interests, and power dynamics of its creators. As such, it is not immune to the systemic biases that exist in society it can absorb, reinforce, and even amplify them. Since AI systems is crucial for the good of humanity, individuals, societies and the environment and ecosystems, there is need for trustworthiness and integrity of the life arising from AI ethical issues. The researcher recommended further study on AI and emotional attachment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Ethics; Human dignity; Implication; Value

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to help support decision making. The benefits to using AI may depend on how much trust, understanding and perceived usefulness there is toward the recommendations. In this study, we look into the relationship between trust in AI, perceived explainable AI, perceived usefulness, human-AI collaboration and perceived decision quality. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted to gather data, with 201 responses recorded. Each construct was calculated by finding the mean of five Likert scale questions. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation and multiple regression were performed. The means of the constructs ranged from 4.07 to 4.16. The Cronbach's alphas ranged from 0.506 to 0.617. The first regression model showed that 48.8% of the variation in human-AI collaboration could be explained. The second regression model shows a positive relationship between trust in AI, explainable AI, perceived usefulness, and perceived decision quality. The adjusted coefficient for human-AI collaboration was not statistically significant at .05. Due to the low internal consistency and inconsistencies in the screening questions for AI use in the spreadsheet, this is an exploratory study and should be treated with caution.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) has created new opportunities for accessibility, communication, and independent learning for students who are hearing-impaired. Such students may face barriers in understanding spoken instructions in the classroom, participating in oral discussions, grasping complex academic terminology, interacting with hearing peers, and accessing educational resources independently. Traditional assistive technologies, such as hearing aids, cochlear implants, captioning systems, speech-to-text applications, and digital learning platforms, have contributed significantly to educational accessibility. However, recent advancements in Generative AI have opened up new possibilities through AI-based conversational assistants, automated text generation, language simplification, real-time transcription, personalized explanations, summarization, and interactive learning support. This study aims to examine the potential impact of Generative AI on the communication and independent learning skills of hearing-impaired students. The research focuses on three key aspects: communication skills, independent learning skills, and students' perceptions regarding the utility and accessibility of Generative AI tools. A quantitative research approach is adopted, using a quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test control-group design. Additionally, qualitative feedback has been gathered from both students and teachers. A sample of 100 hearing-impaired students is divided into two groups, an experimental group and a control group, with 50 students in each. The experimental group receives structured learning support through Generative AI tools, while the control group is provided with traditional instruction and learning support. Data collection involved the use of standardized or researcher-developed assessment tools, observation schedules, and student feedback questionnaires. To test the research hypotheses, the study employs descriptive statistics (including mean and standard deviation), as well as paired-sample t-tests, independent-sample t-tests, and effect-size analysis. The paper argues that well-designed and monitored Generative AI interventions can provide students with enhanced opportunities to express their ideas, comprehend academic information, access learning materials, develop self-directed learning habits, and participate with greater confidence in an inclusive educational environment. It also highlights concerns related to AI accuracy, accessibility, privacy, digital inequality, linguistic diversity, and over-reliance. The study emphasizes that Generative AI should function as a supportive and collaborative educational tool, not as a replacement for teachers, sign language interpreters, or established modes of human interaction and communication.

documents.abstract: The field of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is now receiving much attention and is being utilised in areas such as writing, investigation, design, programming and data and client services. Generative AI can develop text, graphics and other content according to user instruction. Its increasing implementation in business and education has led to both enthusiasm and concern, particularly amongst students as they consider their own future careers. Whilst a degree and/or knowledge is still important in the workplace, there is increasing recognition of the value of applied skills. Digital skills, problem solving, communication and the ability to utilise and learn how to use new technology are also highly regarded. Although AI can automate parts of some jobs, it is also seen as an enabler, allowing staff to work in new and more efficient ways. Again, this will vary depending on a job and how and to what extent AI is implemented and used by an organisation and its staff. India’s government and industry are currently addressing and responding to the above trends. Literature produced by these bodies frequently references building AI skills, re-skilling and ensuring young people can adjust to evolving career roles. Thus, this research looks at how students can adjust to working in an AI enhanced world and considers what universities may need to do to facilitate this.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied for corporate communication, but organizations lack clear guidance on how human communication professionals and AI systems, tools, and platforms should collaborate for creativity in this field. This article presents findings from a conceptual research paper that introduces a Human–AI Co-Creation Framework. The novel perspective highlights eight factors for successful co-creation across three levels: individual, organizational, and societal.

Knowledge worker productivity (KWP) is increasingly challenged by information overload, interruptions, technostress, and growing cognitive complexity. This systematic literature review synthesizes research from information systems (IS), psychology, organizational behavior, and knowledge management to examine cognitive, behavioral, and technology-related mechanisms shaping individual KWP. Following a search of Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, 89 studies were included and analyzed using a hybrid deductive–inductive thematic synthesis. The findings identify three interrelated dimensions: cognitive mechanisms, including attention, cognitive flexibility, memory, creativity, and cognitive load; behavioral self-management processes, including situation analysis, goal setting, action planning, resource identification, action implementation, evaluation, and motivation; and technology-related strain, including technology overload, techno-invasion, and technostress. Building on these findings, the review develops an IS research agenda comprising six avenues: productivity monitoring and sensing, goal and habit support, knowledge extraction, personalized digital interventions, learning support, and productivity-based recommendations and systems integration. Unlike prior single-mechanism reviews, this review integrates cognitive, behavioral, and technology-related perspectives into one framework of individual KWP and links each research avenue to its evidence. The findings imply that productivity-oriented IS should support self-regulation while mitigating technology-related strain and preserving autonomy and privacy; many artificial-intelligence-based solutions still await empirical validation.

documents.abstract: Despite the growing integration of AI technologies in Ethiopian education, the synthesis of studies on outcomes, benefits, and challenges is limited. This study aims to address this gap. A systematic search of databases, search engines, repositories, and other sources produced 850 studies, of which 13 were reported. Accordingly, AI initiatives address both education about AI and AI-supported educational practice. Generative and conversational AI systems were integrated across student-centered learning, administrative, assessment, and decision-making activities, alongside increasing emphasis on embedding AI concepts within curricula and broader institutional frameworks. Its multi-level transformation includes improving personalized learning trajectories, teaching efficiency, and instructional quality, as well as systemic operation and data-informed decision-making. They promise (a) adaptive learning experiences through immediate feedback and content modulation, (b) efficiency gains through automation of routine academic and administrative tasks, and (c) broader systemic benefits, including access to learning resources and reduction of structural inequities. However, infrastructural limits, digital literacy deficits, limited comprehensive governance for ethical integration, and other contextual challenges, such as cultural, linguistic, and institutional features, restricted the realization of the promises. Collectively, the findings imply that AI in education (AIEd) is not a neutral supporting tool, but rather a socio-technical mediation whose effect depends on technological skill, institutional readiness, and context alignment.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrating into the system of secondary vocational education within the context of digital transformation. The gap between AI's potential and the lack of specific pedagogical methods creates a critical need for personnel with advanced digital competencies. This research synthesizes sociological data with a pedagogical experiment designed to identify the difficulties experienced by instructors and students when integrating effective AI options into a professionally oriented educational environment. The pedagogical experiment was conducted at the Ural Technological College, a branch of the National Research Nuclear University MEPhI (Moscow Engineering Physics Institute). The study utilized questionnaires, interviews, and expert evaluations of AI-assisted tasks in Mathematics and English. While the students demonstrated interest and readiness to use AI in practice, their overall level of AI literacy remained low, revealing a utilitarian and uncritical approach. Furthermore, although the didactic advantages of AI include personalization, prompt engineering opportunities, and the development of critical thinking, the instructors’ methodological deficits combined with the students’ low AI literacy formed a vicious circle. Consequently, effective AI utilization requires mandatory, structured pedagogical support rather than spontaneous implementation. Ideally, students should develop critical AI literacy while instructors transition into methodologists and tutors, with both parties adhering to clear institutional regulations. Such a comprehensive approach transforms AI from a source of risk into a sustainable.

documents.abstract: This study aims to investigate primary school teachers’ views on the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in science education, focusing on their perceived readiness and views on their teaching practices. Such views matter because teachers’ perceptions shape their readiness and practices and can inform the design of professional development programs. A questionnaire on perceived readiness informed by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) was administered to 319 future and in-service teachers to measure levels of perceived readiness to use GenAI. To explore the reasons that encourage or discourage teachers from incorporating GenAI in their science teaching, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 teachers. On average, participants reported moderately positive attitudes towards GenAI in science education and moderate self-assessed competence, but perceived their training as insufficient and expressed considerable concerns about barriers to its use, while in-service teachers’ views on available resources were neutral. Collectively, they recognize multiple opportunities and impediments associated with its utilization, which encourage or deter them from using GenAI for science teaching, respectively. However, these reasons mainly concerned teachers’ preparation (e.g., lesson planning) and domain-general capabilities and challenges; science-specific affordances and risks were raised by only a few participants.

This study aims to analyze, from a critical-analytical perspective, the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the field of Instructional Design (ID) within the contemporary educational context, articulating pedagogical, technological, and ethical dimensions. The investigation is grounded in thetheoretical premise that the integration of intelligent systems into the planning, development, andevaluation of learning experiences constitutes a structural transformation in ID practices, rather thanmerely a technological expansion of resources. The central theoretical framework draws on Filatro’s(2008) contributions to Instructional Design, Russell and Norvig’s (2021) foundations of AI, Luckin etal.’s (2016) work on AI in education, and Bates’s (2019) research on learning in digital environments, articulated within a constructivist perspective and the premises of meaningful learning. Methodologically, the research is qualitative, bibliographical, and exploratory in nature, guided by acritical analysis of specialized literature with explicit source selection criteria. The analyticalcategories employed are: learning personalization, pedagogical mediation, teacher autonomy, dataethics, and pedagogical intentionality. Results show that AI significantly expands the possibilities forcurricular adaptation and performance monitoring through learning analytics, but does not replaceInstructional Design. Rather, it redefines the instructional designer’s role, demanding more sophisticated analytical, strategic, and ethical competencies capable of ensuring the centrality of the learningsubject and the pedagogical coherence of educational proposals.

documents.abstract: This research analyzes the ethical and legal challenges related to the use of Artificial Intelligence in recruitment and selection processes, based on the case of the experimental tool developed by Amazon. The objective is to understand the problems highlighted by this episode and identify lessons that may contribute to the more responsible use of these technologies in Brazilian organizations. To this end, the study adopted a qualitative approach, combining a literature review with a case study based on publicly available sources. The analysis drew on academic literature, news coverage of the case, and Brazilian legislation. The results showed that the use of historical data and inadequate criteria may contribute to the reproduction of algorithmic biases and negatively affect the evaluation of certain candidates. Challenges related to system transparency, human oversight, and organizational responsibility were also identified. It is concluded that the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in recruitment and selection processes requires planning, continuous monitoring, and attention to personal data protection and equal opportunities, so that technology serves as a support tool for human resource management without replacing organizational responsibility.

documents.abstract: AI agents now read and change files, run commands and open network connections on the computers of the people who use them, and the operating system authorizes every one of these actions as the user, because it has no notion of an agent. A single injected instruction or misjudged step therefore reaches every credential, document and connection the user can reach. We present IOArx, which makes the agent the principal of access control on the endpoint without changing agents, models or the kernel. IOArx names the agent behind each kernel event by following the process chain to verified code-signing evidence, decides the event with a policy written for agents, pauses or stops the agent's entire process tree when the policy asks or forbids, refuses forbidden connections at their first packet, and inspects prompts, pastes and uploads before they reach AI chat services. We formalize the policy and prove that its decisions are deterministic, that rules for ordinary programs cannot grant an agent access, that added rules move decisions monotonically, that remembered answers bound the number of prompts, and how much an agent can still do before it is held; we also derive the exact error rates of the checksum and entropy validation in the prompt detectors. On a developer workstation, IOArx attributed 36 processes to their agents, 16 of them through their ancestors, without a single misattribution, and recognized no program outside an agent product among 3{,}449 executables. On Linux it stopped a violating agent within a median of 3.1~ms, a complete decision takes 19~μs, and on 32{,}771 real user prompts the default detectors raised no false alarm while finding 99.65\% of the credentials and personal data planted in them.

Background Educational digitalization and generative artificial intelligence are changing how theoretical education organizes curricula, represents knowledge, structures learning interactions, and conducts assessment. AI is moving beyond an auxiliary role in content provision, resource recommendation, and performance prediction to become an infrastructure that participates in explanation, collaboration, feedback, and judgment. Yet this literature remains dispersed across educational technology, teacher education, medicine and nursing, engineering education, and language education. Existing reviews therefore provide only a partial account of its macro-development, knowledge structure, and temporal evolution. Methods We searched Web of Science and Scopus for publications dated from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2025. The search yielded 7,818 raw records, comprising 2,527 records from Web of Science and 5,291 from Scopus. Date and document-type restrictions, cross-database deduplication, title and abstract screening, and thematic eligibility review produced a final corpus of 1,489 publications. Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and BERTopic were fitted to the same corpus. Annual topic aggregation, prevalence analysis, cross-model alignment, and bibliometric auditing were then combined to identify the field's knowledge structure and evolutionary pathways. Results Publication growth was modest between 2016 and 2020 but accelerated after 2023, increasing from 344 records in 2024 to 816 in 2025. LDA identified 14 broad topics spanning institutional transformation and curriculum development, generative AI integration, AI-mediated assessment, writing, and critical thinking, professional education, teacher development, personalized learning, technology acceptance, virtual simulation, and AI literacy and ethics. BERTopic identified 14 substantive clusters. Its largest interpretable cluster, AI-enabled pedagogy, literacy, and ethics, contained 416 records and accounted for 27.94% of the full corpus. A further 494 records were assigned to Other/outlier (33.18%), indicating substantial interdisciplinary heterogeneity. The temporal evidence showed reorganization rather than displacement: online learning, intelligent feedback, curriculum development, and virtual simulation were re-embedded within generative interaction, assessment evidence, learner agency, and platform governance. Conclusion AI-empowered theoretical education has developed from a collection of discrete technology applications into a sociotechnical field organized around curricula, educational actors, evidence, ethics, and professional practice. Future research should address six connected priorities: learner agency and AI literacy, collaborative knowledge construction, platform governance and educational equity, teacher and curriculum capacity, traceable assessment evidence, and domain-sensitive transfer between theory and practice. The study provides an auditable, cross-database, dual-model framework for monitoring knowledge structures, thematic reorganization, and the boundaries of this emerging field.

documents.abstract: Leaders' effectiveness depends not only on skills and motivation but also on personal resources that sustain energy and well-being beyond work. Yet research on leaders' non-work-related personal resources (NWPR) remains scattered across leadership, occupational health, and recovery literatures. To address this fragmentation, we combine topic modeling with integrative synthesis to conduct the first systematic review dedicated to leader NWPR. We analyze 312 articles and synthesize NWPR topics within a Context–Mechanisms–Outcomes framework. Findings show that the intellectual structure of leader NWPR research is highly fragmented, spanning eight theoretical domains. These diverse literatures converge in viewing leaders' recovery and well-being outside work as indispensable for sustaining effective leadership. Our integrative framework goes beyond descriptive synthesis by specifying how leadership contexts may activate or constrain NWPR mechanisms across time and levels. The framework positions leadership as a contextual amplifier: because leaders occupy roles of sustained visibility, accountability, and relational influence, their restored or depleted resource states may be enacted through interaction and may cascade to followers, teams, and organizations. It identifies three temporally nested mechanism pathways: daily depletion–replenishment, cumulative resource gain–loss dynamics, and cross-domain transfer with relational amplification. Through these pathways, off-job resources may shape leader well-being, leadership behavior, and multilevel outcomes. We also assess the causal trustworthiness of links between the framework's categories. Our synthesis provides a coherent foundation, propositions, and a research agenda for understanding how leaders' off-job personal resources may support well-being, ethical behavior, and enduring performance.

Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, university students’ digital literacy (DL) has become an important concern in higher education. Drawing on social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this study examined the association between artificial intelligence literacy (AIL) and DL and the parallel mediating roles of information literacy self-efficacy (ILSE), SRL, and learning motivation (LM). Methods A questionnaire survey recruited university students in mainland China and yielded 504 cases for analysis. Measures included adapted versions of the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, a 16-item self-report DL scale covering eight domains, the Chinese-revised Information Literacy Self-Efficacy Scale, the Learners’ Self-Regulated Learning Ability Self-Report Scale, and the motivation section of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0, AMOS 26.0, and semopy 2.3.11. Results AIL showed a positive direct association with DL after all three mediators were included simultaneously (B = 0.233, 95% CI [0.114, 0.363]). The specific indirect effects through ILSE, SRL, and LM were 0.097 (95% CI [0.046, 0.168]), 0.054 (95% CI [0.010, 0.109]), and 0.077 (95% CI [0.027, 0.144]), respectively. None of the confidence intervals included zero. Discussion The findings inform the design of digital learning tasks in higher education, including guided AI skills practice, feedback on challenging tasks, support for goal setting and progress monitoring, and connections to students’ academic interests and future careers. The cross-sectional design and nonprobability sampling limit causal inference and generalizability.

Are large language models (LLMs) bad at capturing human judgment? Two commonly stated limitations are that LLMs fail to capture full distributions of responses, and that their judgments are unstable across wording variations. We demonstrate simple prompting strategies that mitigate these limitations. Across two datasets—a U.S.-representative set of 144 moral scenarios and 38 moral beliefs from the International Social Survey Programme's Family and Changing Gender Roles module covering 32 countries—we show how simple elicitation techniques help improve AI-human alignment. First, prompting models to report standard deviations and response proportions recovers the full range of human responses better than common strategies. Second, ensuring scenarios are clear to human participants—as reflected in human confusion ratings—is associated with stronger model alignment, and LLMs can track human confusion ratings. At the same time, we find that model confidence ratings do not consistently track errors in models' judgments, though they can predict human variability relatively well. These results suggest that asking better questions to LLMs can yield better answers.
