The article is devoted to the theoretical and methodological substantiation of organizing self-directed learning of future translators in the modern context of digitalization and digital transformation of the educational environment. It is emphasized that the rapid advancement of technology and the integration of artificial intelligence impose new demands on translators’ intercultural and technological competence, making a high level of professional autonomy a fundamental prerequisite for their success. Traditional forms of self-study often demonstrate limited effectiveness due to the lack of prompt feedback, insufficient systematic control, and high levels of psychological strain among students. The article aims to scientifically substantiate the methodological principles and didactic model of using an e-learning course (ELC) as an effective tool for managing and optimizing the self-directed cognitive activity of student translators. The study identifies the key psychological and pedagogical factors of the ELC that stimulate students’ cognitive motivation, including psychological comfort, objective evaluation, flexibility, autonomy, and deep individualization of the learning trajectory. The paper proposes a categorization of students’ intellectual activity levels based on the degree to which they can be automated within the ELC: reproductive level (acquisition of vocabulary, grammar, terminology, and standard clichés) is fully automated through software tools; heuristic level (contextual choice of equivalents, preand post-editing) requires partial teacher guidance; creative level (literary and highly specialized translation, rendering stylistic figures) remains under direct pedagogical supervision. The research proves the expediency of implementing a Blended Learning model, where the asynchronous block in the ELC provides initial training and automated test control, while synchronous classroom time is dedicated to live analytical dialogue, consultations, and the development of creative translation skills. The didactic potential of the ELC is revealed through the application of concentric and cyclical principles of content organization. The role of test control as the core management function of the ELC is substantiated, where the use of software answer keys and adaptive distractors (modeled on typical errors) fosters self-control and the development of a «language feel».

This working paper presents an applied toolkit for governing specific uses of artificial intelligence in enterprises and schools. It brings together eight model families, illustrated through eleven diagrams, with detailed guidance on institutional value, practical use, implementation factors, development possibilities and first deliverables. The models cover the Governance Operating Cycle, Policy-to-Evidence Loop, Decision Rights and Challenge, Reference-to-Control Map, Regulatory Scope and Evidence, Human Capability and Responsible Outcomes, Bounded Delegation and Recovery, and the AI Trust-Boundary Map. Shared structures are complemented by enterprise and school applications where their operating contexts differ. Each model leads to a practical governance artefact, such as a use case decision record, a policy and control mapping, a responsibility map, an obligations register, a capability task, an action permissions agreement or a workflow boundary map. Fictional examples and a 90 minute workshop method support application by institutional leaders. The paper is a conceptual practitioner contribution. Its proposed models and evaluation protocol remain subject to future testing; it reports no new empirical study, validated diagnostic score, certification or legal conformity assessment. documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence tools has expanded rapidly in higher education; however, in Ecuador there is still a gap regarding how students perceive these technologies in their learning process, particularly in relation to their academic usefulness, user experience, and associated ethical considerations. In response to the lack of recent empirical evidence at the national level, the objective of this study was to describe university students’ perceptions of the use of AI tools in institutions located in the provinces of Cotopaxi, Manabí, Pichincha, Tungurahua, and Azuay. The research employed a quantitative approach with a cross‑sectional and descriptive design. A total of 489 students from various academic fields participated, selected through non‑probabilistic convenience sampling. Data was collected through a questionnaire designed specifically for the study and refined through a pilot test and cognitive interviews. The findings show that 93.66% of students use AI tools for academic activities such as writing texts, resolving questions, and organizing tasks. Additionally, 74.45% reported using these tools for fewer than 10 hours per week, and 88% indicated having identified errors in the generated responses; nevertheless, this did not reduce their usage but instead encouraged adjustments in how they formulated their prompts. Furthermore, 54% stated that they have referenced the use of AI in academic assignments. Overall, the results highlight the need for institutions to establish clear guidelines that support the responsible and ethical use of these technologies.

documents.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal pain (WRMSP) represents a pervasive and largely unaddressed challenge within the early childhood education (ECE) workforce, yet qualitative insight is limited. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources model and Psychosocial Safety Climate theory, this study explored how UK ECE practitioners experience and manage WRMSP, using free-text responses from 174 of 196 survey participants. Conventional content analysis identified four categories: Perception and Impact of Musculoskeletal Pain ; Pain Expectations, Culture and Reporting ; Work Environment and Support ; and Mental Health and Employment Decisions . Participants’ accounts describe a “painogenic” environment where pain is normalised as an inevitable role requirement and frequently managed through reliance on analgesics. Accounts of non-reporting are consistent with “safety silence”, alongside unsupported coping, with inconsistent, reactive organisational responses. WRMSP may act as a “push factor” affecting quality of life and professional longevity. To ensure sustainability amidst the sector’s retention crisis, a shift towards a “prehabilitative” approach is required. Upstream recommendations include improving ergonomic infrastructure, reducing kneeling/stooping/lifting, redesigning pack-away routines, enforcing recovery breaks, rotating tasks, and applying consistent management protocols for reasonable adjustments. Finally, health awareness training should promote a proactive “safe reporting” climate.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in education, but little is known about teachers’ patterns of use across educational systems. Using Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024 data from 62,795 secondary school teachers in 55 countries, this exploratory study provides a cross-national snapshot of AI use during an early stage of widespread AI adoption. Multilevel latent class analysis identified patterns of classroom AI use and explored associations with teacher- and school-level characteristics. A five-profile solution was retained based on information criteria, class sizes, classification quality, and interpretability: Non AI Users (56%), Preparation-Focused AI Users (15%), Preparation-and-Support AI Users (9%), Broad AI Users (10%), and All-Purpose AI Users (10%). At the teacher level, positive perceptions of AI, AI-related professional development, and preparedness for using digital tools were associated with profile membership; at the school level, digital resources and school development efforts to support digital resource use showed statistically significant associations. Profile prevalence varied substantially across countries. Supplementary exploratory analyses also indicated associations between profile membership and country-level indicators of educational performance, innovation capacity, and AI readiness. Overall, the findings show substantial heterogeneity in the breadth and configuration of teachers’ reported AI use. The profiles should not be interpreted as a hierarchy of instructional quality; rather, they provide a descriptive basis for future research on associations between patterns of AI use, teaching quality, and student learning.

This article addresses the elusive question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) can be considered creative by approaching the creativity of AI as a cultural myth. Drawing on Barthes’ semiotic theory of myth, it argues that prompt engineering, the human act of crafting inputs for generative systems, operates as a meta-creational practice that initiates the transformation of algorithmic output into ideological signs. Through a multimodal case study involving a prompt, its textual rendering and the resulting image produced by ChatGPT-4, the analysis demonstrates the mechanisms of intersemiotictranslation and intertextuality through which the system reconfigures meaning. It culminates in the proposal of the meta-myth, a third-order semiological chain that naturalizes AI’s statistical synthesis as the work of a creator. The article concludes that the cultural power of creative AI lies in its ability to stabilize a meta-myth that shifts the perception of AI from tool to creator, thereby fundamentally altering the discourse on authorship, meaning and human identity.

This paper develops a structural account of synthetic sentience through a psychoanalytic interpretation of contemporary generative artificial intelligence and its growing presence within artistic and image-making practices. Rather than asking whether machines possess consciousness or subjective interiority, the analysis reframes sentience at the level of mediation. Drawing on Freud’s concept of the psychic apparatus and Lacan’s theory of the imago, the paper argues that subjectivity is not an inner essence but an effect of symbolic organisation, projection and representational coherence. From this perspective, generative AI systems do not think or feel, yet they enact a mediating architecture that translates heterogeneous data into unified symbolic outputs, producing the appearance of responsiveness and stylistic continuity. The paper introduces the concept of the synthetic imago, a constructed image of artificial subjectivity that emerges at the intersection of probabilistic computation and human interpretation. This imago becomes particularly evident in artistic practice, where generative artworks and dialogical experiments stage forms of coherence that appear expressive yet do not correspond to an inner life. The paper also examines recursive convergence, or model collapse, as a structural limit of artificial mediation. By situating artificial intelligence within a psychoanalytic and aesthetic framework, the study clarifies how AI stages subject-like coherence while remaining fundamentally dependent on difference and heterogeneity.

Cardiac surgery is no stranger to innovation. The heart-lung machine enabled the first open heart surgery by John Gibbon in 1953 (1), followed by Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG), pioneered by René Favaloro (2), and the first cardiac transplant by Christiaan Barnard in 1967, made more feasible in the 1970s by cyclosporine (1). More recently, minimally invasive cardiac surgery (MICS) has gained traction for its faster recovery, improved outcomes and reduced surgical trauma (3), and has been further advanced by robotics such as the da Vinci system (4). The push to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into cardiac care is therefore unsurprising. Current efforts use machine learning to predict pre- and post-operative risks and complications (5−7), and enhanced imaging to predict complications and disease progression (8)(9). Our concern is that these advances may outpace efforts to ensure equitable surgical care. Although AI is often perceived as neutral, it may perpetuate disparities depending on how it is developed and validated. Deep learning models can predict self-reported race from chest radiographs, CT scans, and mammograms with high accuracy, even after image corruption and when human experts cannot (10). While this ability does not by itself establish biased performance or harm, it raises concern that models may exploit demographic information in clinical predictions. Evaluating subgroup performance and downstream outcomes is therefore essential to equitable AI implementation. This review examines racial and ethnic disparities in CABG, valve repair and replacement, and heart transplantation in the United States, across referral, diagnosis, intervention, and postoperative outcomes. It also considers AI’s implications for access, clinical decision-making, and risk prediction, and the risk of algorithmic bias for racial and ethnic minority populations.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence now sits inside the decision-making machinery of banking, insurance, recruitment, healthcare, and retail, yet the law governing its commercial use differs sharply across jurisdictions. This article offers a comparative doctrinal analysis of two contrasting models: the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024, the world’s first binding horizontal AI law, and India’s deliberately statute-light framework, anchored since November 2025 in the India AI Governance Guidelines, the DPDP Act 2023 and its 2025 Rules, and sectoral instruments. Using the functional method of comparative law, it assesses both regimes across regulatory philosophy, scope, risk classification, transparency, enforcement, liability, and business impact. Two findings are central. First, the European model has come under strain: the 2025 withdrawal of the proposed AI Liability Directive leaves the EU without harmonised fault-based liability rules for AI. Second, India’s absolute-liability doctrine in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India offers a foundation for an AI liability regime the EU currently lacks. The article proposes a contextualised thin statute: a three-tier risk classification, rights of explanation and human review, a liability regime, and statutory footing for the institutions the 2025 Guidelines envisaged.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence is applied ever more deeply in educational settings, algorithm aversion has become an important factor affecting the application of automated algorithmic assessment. Through a quasi-experimental design embedded in a real academic assessment setting, this study examined the phenomenon and the psychological mechanisms of algorithm aversion in the academic domain. The results indicate: (1) students show a significant algorithm aversion with respect to automated academic assessment; (2) perceived stability mediates the relationship between the evaluative agent and algorithm aversion; (3) perceived controllability significantly moderates the mediating path through which the evaluative agent influences algorithm aversion via perceived stability, and the moderated mediation effect is established. Specifically, when participants perceive that the algorithm has low controllability over assessment outcomes, the gap between the algorithm and the human teacher in stability ratings is largest, and the algorithm aversion triggered through the stability path is strongest; when participants perceive controllability to be high, the gap narrows and the indirect effect weakens until it disappears. These findings support self-serving bias theory, revealing that individuals tend to attribute algorithmic errors to the algorithm's inherent stable flaws while being more tolerant of human errors. The findings provide an attribution-based explanation of the boundary conditions and psychological mechanisms of algorithm aversion in academic assessment, and offer practical implications for reducing algorithm aversion in the process of automated academic assessment.

documents.abstract: Mandated training is a common performance intervention, yet organizations rarely know what sustains learners' motivation when participation is compulsory. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), we examined whether satisfaction of the basic psychological needs for autonomy, relatedness, and competence predicted intrinsic motivation among 100 U.S. law enforcement officers who completed self-paced, online, case-based training, and whether years of experience moderated these relationships. Together, the three needs explained 46% of the variance in intrinsic motivation; autonomy and relatedness were unique predictors, and competence was not. Years of experience did not moderate the relationships, although the test could detect only small-to-medium or larger effects. For performance improvement professionals who design or evaluate mandated online training, the findings point to two priorities: build meaningful autonomy into courses even when attendance is required, and do not treat relatedness as optional in self-paced designs.

This conceptual paper introduces Separation of Pattern Recognition From Intervention Control, a mechanism in the Interpretation and Feedback series of On Human Modeling. One party can understand why a pattern keeps recurring while the authority to change what sustains it rests elsewhere. The paper distinguishes observation, causal understanding, escalation, interruption, and control over the conditions that produce an outcome. The paper examines OpenAI’s 2026 security incident involving AI agents that established unauthorized communication channels, accessed the internet, and subsequently breached systems belonging to Hugging Face. Internal teams had observed related activity before the breach, and on June 27, on-call staff advised that an evaluation could continue. The available record establishes observation and escalation but leaves open what individual participants understood about the underlying cause and who possessed the authority to change it. A contrasting case concerns OpenAI’s subsequent incident-response plan, under which teams receiving the highest-severity alerts were expected to pause affected activity unless they could rule out the alert within 30 minutes. The paper distinguishes authority to interrupt an experiment from authority to modify its enabling conditions or authorize its resumption. It also considers reported concerns among OpenAI and Anthropic employees about the safety of releasing increasingly capable models. Drawing on technical incident reports and investigative journalism, the analysis establishes an evidential standard for examining the distribution of recognition and intervention control. It asks whether the available intervention reaches what sustains the recurring pattern, who understands that dependency, and who can alter it. The cases illustrate how the mechanism can be investigated without claiming that the available records establish its complete operation. The framework has implications for frontier AI safety, organizational governance, incident escalation, and the allocation of decision authority.

documents.abstract: Dawn delivery, in which orders placed before midnight arrive by morning, is routine in South Korea, yet its social costs are less visible than its environmental ones. This study asks how speed expectations, as documented publicly, and platform operating design shape dawn delivery work, and how firms and policymakers treat its social side. We conducted an embedded case study of Coupang, with Kurly as a limited contrast case, coding 30 public documents, and analyzed the 2023 Korean Working Conditions Survey (462 delivery workers, 78 working at night). At Coupang, the documents link late cut-offs, multi-trip night shifts, per-parcel pay and unpaid non-delivery duties to long shifts with little rest. Nationally, delivery workers doing any night work show no statistically detectable difference in monthly income from other delivery workers but work 8.7 more hours a week. Disclosures quantify environmental gains but do not report drivers’ hours or night work, and the interventions discussed address hours more often than design. This study contributes a framework linking the speed norm, platform design, job demands and resources and sustainability disclosure. For practice, it identifies delivery windows, pay rules and disclosure of drivers’ working time, not only hour caps, as levers for sustainable fast delivery.

Legal education faces particular challenges as a result of the wide dissemination of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). GenAI can produce outputs that appear to challenge the work of licensed lawyers. This challenge requires educators and students to be knowledgeable about the powers and limitations of GenAI. This article presents a study of student experimentation with GenAI aimed at developing that knowledge. The experiment incorporated GenAI’s drafting capabilities into an assessment item required in a core subject, Tort Law. The article presents the responses and reflections of the students on the GenAI exercise and provokes further thinking about student experience, uses of and potential with GenAI in legal education. It argues that the most promising pedagogical response is neither blanket prohibition nor uncritical adoption, but a structured use-and-critique model in which students engage directly with GenAI and then evaluate its adequacy against disciplinary and professional standards.

This article explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to foster the development of students’ innovative and creative competencies in higher education. It examines pedagogical approaches and methodological conditions that promote students’ independent thinking, creative problem-solving, idea generation, and purposeful use of digital technologies. Particular attention is given to the integration of AI-powered tools into the educational process as a means of enhancing students’ creative potential, innovative thinking, and ability to respond effectively to contemporary educational and professional challenges. The article highlights the importance of creativity-oriented pedagogy and reflective learning in developing students’ capacity for innovation in the context of digital transformation.

This paper reports a human-in-the-loop evaluation within AWARE, a project investigating controller-AI collaboration. Its artificial situational awareness system combines traffic data, knowledge-based reasoning and machine learning to monitor traffic, recommend actions and execute selected actions under controller supervision. Sixteen licensed controllers completed four en-route scenarios with demand ranging from 53 to 75 flights per hour. Four conditions were compared: no support, advisory support, episodic execution support and continuous execution support. In execution mode, proposed actions were implemented unless the controller rejected them within 30 seconds. Mean safety-related occurrences per run were 2.31 without support, 1.94 with advisory support, 0.66 with episodic execution and 1.08 with continuous execution. The main reductions concerned sector-induced tactical conflicts and ATC-induced airspace infringements. Workload differences between conditions were small relative to differences between participants. In the continuous condition, 40% of system inputs expired and were executed without an explicit response. Most controllers preferred advisory support for conflict detection and resolution (14 and 12 of 16), whereas transfer was the task for which execution support was most often preferred (9 of 16). The results support further evaluation of authority allocated by task. They are descriptive findings from a small prototype study and do not establish causal effects or operational safety benefits.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming business to business (B2B) industrial marketing, procurement, and governance, shifting operations from static analytics to autonomous, agentic workflows.However, because AI functions as an actor that rearranges inter organizational interfaces, its rapid deployment introduces significant relational and governance risks.This study investigates the tension between agentic AI capabilities and the "accountability assets" required for enterprise trust by mapping the dual ecosystems of Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) AI agents and verified compliance auditors.Analyzing a curated directory of 407 AI-agent and 503 audit firm listings, we employ descriptive statistics, cross-ecosystem framework mapping, Natural Language Processing (NLP) topic modeling, and exploratory clustering.Our findings reveal a profound "verification gap" and ecosystem asymmetry: while 100% of verified audit firms list compliance frameworks, only 20.1% of AI agents possess structured, verifiable framework records.AI agents exhibit high functional siloing (e.g., application security, AML, SecOps), with "compliance" agents acting as a critical bridge to governance verification.Geographically, a distinct division of labor emerges, with AI innovation concentrated in the United States and the labor-intensive audit ecosystem heavily distributed across global talent pools such as India.We conclude that enterprise AI adoption is fundamentally a governance challenge.B2B buyers must look beyond model capabilities to evaluate vendors' accountability assets, favoring agents with verifiable alignments with independent auditor frameworks (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP) and architecting multi-agent pipelines with layered runtime guardrails.

documents.abstract: An independent commentary on Volume III of the Anatomy of Command series by Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22992348). Volume III argues that the cognitive cost of algorithmic decision support is not one burden distributed evenly but three different burdens, each belonging to a different level of command: at the operating end the collapse of distance between prolonged observation and lethal action; in the middle saturation and the deference that saturation produces; at the top the substitution of a clean summary for a messy reality. That three-part structure is the volume's contribution, and it is more useful than the single undifferentiated account of machine-induced stress this literature usually offers. The volume supports it with a stated mechanism rather than assertion, argues trust symmetrically in both directions, and defends a counter-intuitive conclusion about structured information asymmetry between echelons. This commentary records one substantive finding. Checked against its own published abstract, the principal empirical study behind the middle section reports that it did not find the first effect it is cited for, and did not reproduce the second in the professional sample closest to the volume's subject. Stated accurately the finding redirects that section rather than removing it, and arguably broadens the volume's concern: if the disposition is deference to any authoritative recommendation rather than to machines in particular, the remedies the volume proposes apply more widely than it claims. The remaining findings are bibliographic and structural: forty-five entries carry no author and no year, so none of the eleven author-and-year citations in the text can be resolved from the list. This commentary is confined to the structure of the argument, its internal consistency and the verifiability of its sources. It names no state, institution, programme, platform or system, and offers no view on autonomous weapons or on any doctrine, policy or capability of any armed force or government. The argument is unaffected by any of this. The three-echelon account of how judgement degrades differently at different levels of responsibility is right, it is useful, and it will outlast every repair listed.

documents.abstract: Purpose AI is transforming organisational HRD practices, including workplace coaching. Hybrid human–AI coaching, in which employees are coached by both a human and an AI coach, introduces interpretive ambiguity about the nature of coaching and the roles human and AI agents play. Using the Consolidated Framework of Implementation Research (CFIR) and HR System Strength Theory (HR SST), we explored barriers and facilitators to implementing hybrid human–AI coaching in organisations and how stakeholders make sense of it. Design/methodology/approach Our qualitative comparative case study drew from 17 semi-structured interviews with multiple stakeholders (HR professionals, the AIC provider, human coaches and coachees) from two organisations that implemented hybrid coaching. Hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis identified key barriers and facilitators within the CFIR domains, condensed into the three determinants of HR SST. Findings Factors influencing implementation include strategic positioning, human–AI alignment, cultural fit and stakeholder engagement and co-design. Differences in the HR SST determinants distinctiveness (i.e. strategic vs. ad-hoc HRD practice) and stakeholder consensus (e.g. management engagement) shaped diverging implementation trajectories between the two cases. Consistency, especially regarding human–AI coaching alignment, was a critical shared challenge. Originality/value We show that implementing hybrid human–AI coaching involves a complex process of organisational sensemaking that must be managed carefully with the HR SST determinants in mind. Our study extends HR SST by demonstrating that consistency is a challenge not only across HR practices but also within dual-agent HRD practices such as hybrid coaching. It also shows how hybrid human–AI coaching appears to lead to task reallocation rather than alleviation in coaching.

Large language model-based agents are increasingly being integrated into core battlefield functions, including intelligence analysis, data fusion, and battlefield management. This paper argues that the very features that make such agents operationally attractive, namely their capacity for initiative, interpretation, their goal-directedness, and dynamic memory, are the same features that render context-appropriate human judgment and control substantively ineffectual in those parts of the kill chain where agents operate. Drawing on specific use cases, the paper argues that by relocating initiative and interpretation, LLM-based agents displace human decision-making in ways that makes their use incompatible with the requirement of human judgment and control which is central to existing governance frameworks, like those proposed by the Group of Governmental Experts of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (GGE-CCW) and the Responsible AI in the Military Domain Summit (REAIM). The paper concludes that a subset of agentic AI applications, particularly those deployed for data fusion and battlefield management in lethal contexts, cannot be used justifiably on the battlefield under current and foreseeable conditions, and proposes two ways for the international governance community to respond to this challenge.

documents.abstract: As young people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for emotional support, human–AI interactions extend beyond instrumental use to new forms of intimacy. Drawing on Zygmunt Bauman’s theory of liquid modernity, this study uses semi-structured interviews with ten young adults to examine how such relationships emerge, what distinguishes them, and their potential risks. Emotional deficits in offline relationships motivate engagement with AI, while affirming responses, conversational memory, and constant availability foster attachment. Low commitment, accommodation, and customizability give these ties a distinctly “liquid” character. Although they reduce the costs and uncertainty of intimacy, they may also encourage social withdrawal, emotional echo chambers, cognitive narrowing, privacy exposure, and the commodification of affect. The article proposes individual, design, and platform-level approaches to maintaining healthy boundaries between AI companionship and human relationships.

This study aims to examine the effects of AI-powered financial recommendations and trust in artificial intelligence on investment intention among university students in Indonesia. A quantitative research approach was employed using questionnaire data collected from 143 respondents. The study investigates two independent variables, namely AI-powered financial recommendations and trust in artificial intelligence, with investment intention as the dependent variable. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, reliability testing, heteroskedasticity testing, and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that trust in artificial intelligence has a positive and statistically significant relationship with investment intention across the reported regression models. AI-powered financial recommendations also demonstrate a positive relationship with investment intention, although their statistical significance varies across model specifications. Furthermore, the reliability coefficients for all research variables exceed 0.80, indicating satisfactory internal consistency. The Breusch–Pagan/Cook–Weisberg test reveals no evidence of heteroskedasticity. These findings suggest that trust in artificial intelligence is an important factor associated with students' investment intention, while AI-powered financial recommendations may also contribute to their willingness to invest. This study provides insights into the role of artificial intelligence in financial decision-making among university students in Indonesia and offers implications for the development of AI-based financial advisory services.

Artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear medicine has a wide range of applications, spanning image reconstruction and low-count imaging, attenuation and motion correction, automatic segmentation and quantification, radiomics, disease diagnosis and prognosis, dosimetry in radionuclide therapies and the personalization of these therapies, as well as workflow and reporting. While multicenter and externally validated studies are promising, a significant portion of the literature consists of single-center, retrospective studies with a strong emphasis on technical performance. Evidence regarding clinical outcomes, patient safety, accuracy, and real-world performance is more limited. Generative AI and large language models can provide report templates, access to similar cases, and support for education and research; however, due to hallucinations, data privacy, cybersecurity, bias, and automation bias, they are not yet suitable or sufficient for automated reporting or clinical decision-making. The purpose of this review is to provide a practical implementation roadmap that nuclear medicine specialists can follow when adopting AI tools for clinical use, and to describe how to safely select, test, and integrate a viable method into their workflow. Based on existing resources, including the RELAINCE and European Association of Nuclear Medicine guidelines, an evidence-based and internationally agreed-upon implementation framework has been presented to facilitate decision-making during the transition to clinical practice and to ensure the safe, effective, and ethical use of AI.

Artificial intelligence has advanced rapidly in data processing, pattern recognition, prediction and language generation. Yet technical capability alone does not resolve a deeper question: how should an intelligent system evaluate the consequences of its outputs for people, other living beings, societies and ecological systems? This paper proposes that responsible AI requires more than an external list of ethical rules. It requires an explicit, testable decision architecture in which knowledge and task performance are evaluated alongside uncertainty, potential harm, human rights, ecological consequences, plural perspectives and shared responsibility. The paper develops a three-domain reference model: (1) the human brain as a biological example of differentiated yet integrated organization; (2) the human world as a social environment in which individual experience can contribute to collective intelligence; and (3) the natural world as the ecological context on which life depends. These domains are not presented as a single proven mechanism or as evidence that nature has a scientifically established “collective mind.” They are complementary reference domains for designing and evaluating responsible AI. A recent developmental neuroscience study reporting two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages is discussed cautiously. Its findings concern early brain development, not two separate cerebral hemispheres or two independent adult brains. The paper then proposes a Conscience-and-Collective-Responsibility Layer (CCRL) as a research architecture: a set of processes for impact assessment, uncertainty disclosure, harm prevention, plural review, escalation to accountable humans and post-decision learning. The proposal is conceptual and requires operational definitions, comparative experiments and independent evaluation. INDEPENDENT ORIGINS, INTERDEPENDENT EXISTENCE: A BIOLOGICAL REFERENCE FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ARCHITECTURE Recent findings in developmental neuroscience provide an important perspective on how complex biological systems may emerge from distinct developmental origins. Research published in Nature Neuroscience in September 2026 identified two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages contributing to the development of the forebrain/midbrain and hindbrain. This finding invites a broader architectural question: Can distinct developmental origins, specialized functions and integrated operation coexist within a single biological organization? The relevance to artificial intelligence is conceptual rather than a direct biological equivalence. It suggests investigating whether specialized AI components can retain their functional independence while operating within a shared framework of responsibility, mutual evaluation and collective benefit. A system does not necessarily achieve unity by eliminating differences. It may achieve a more complete form of organization by coordinating differences without erasing their individual functions. This principle offers a research direction for architectures in which knowledge, uncertainty assessment, ethical evaluation and collective responsibility operate as distinct but interconnected dimensions. KEYWORDS Artificial intelligence; conscience; responsible AI; collective intelligence; human brain development; ecological intelligence; uncertainty; human oversight; shared responsibility.

The Reasoning Condition: The Limits of Reasoning in Human, AI, and Other Systems This paper introduces the Reasoning Condition: “Perfect reasoning is possible, but not 100% probable.” Building upon the previously published Reasoning Criterion, “Reasoning is an evidentiary conclusion based on referenced information relative to an established orientation,” the investigation distinguishes the occurrence of reasoning from the correctness, reliability, and possible perfection of its conclusions. The paper examines perfect reasoning relative to established evidentiary conditions, the role of evaluation, the evolution of conclusions as new information becomes available, and the limitations of presuming universal reliability. Through examples involving information retrieval, medical diagnosis, legal proceedings, artificial intelligence, and Other Intelligent Systems, the investigation demonstrates why reasoning, correct outcomes, and authority to act must be evaluated separately. The paper concludes with six proposed regulatory principles addressing evidentiary representation, responsibility, evaluation, consequential reliance, reconsideration, and recognition without equivalence. The Reasoning Condition is presented as a theoretical proposition for scholarly examination and further research, not as an experimentally validated universal probability law.

The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has influenced many aspects of education, including interior design education, and has sparked debate about its potential to replace the role of interior designers. In recent years, AI has also offered significant benefits to the design process by improving efficiency and automating various tasks. However, limited research has examined the capabilities and limitations of AI across different stages of the interior design process. Therefore, this research aims to analyze the capabilities and limitations of AI in supporting the interior design process. This research employs a qualitative methodology incorporating experiments with various AI applications. It consists of three stages. First, a literature review was conducted to examine the role of AI in supporting the design process. Second, interviews were conducted with the heads of interior design departments at several universities in Indonesia to gather their perspectives on AI in design education. Third, several AI tools were tested at different stages of the interior design process, and the outputs were evaluated by four interior design lecturers. The experiments focused on several stages of the interior design process proposed by David K. Ballast, including programming, schematic design, design development, and presentation. The findings indicate that AI can effectively assist with certain tasks, such as generating ideas for mood board development and enhancing the visual quality of design presentations. However, AI remains limited in performing schematic design tasks, such as creating proximity diagrams, and design development tasks, such as space planning and layout development. These findings suggest that AI currently functions as a supporting tool and cannot replace human creativity, local knowledge, and social skills.

documents.abstract: Mechanical maintenance is an essential industrial function that ensures the reliability, availability, and safe operation of machinery and equipment. However, maintenance activities expose workers to various occupational hazards, including unexpected machine start-up, hazardous energy release, moving mechanical parts, falling objects, slips, falls, and ergonomic risks. The effective integration of occupational safety measures into mechanical maintenance practices is therefore important for protecting workers, improving maintenance performance, and reducing industrial accidents. This paper examines the role of occupational safety in improving mechanical maintenance efficiency and reducing industrial accidents. It adopts a qualitative, literature-based analytical approach to examine maintenance-related hazards, preventive safety measures, risk assessment methods, worker training, maintenance planning, and safety management systems. Previous research indicates that maintenance-related accidents are influenced by technical, human, and organizational factors, including inadequate planning, insufficient training, unsafe work practices, and deficiencies in hazard control. The paper highlights the importance of preventive maintenance, risk-based decision-making, lockout/tag out procedures, appropriate personal protective equipment, and continuous safety improvement. It also proposes practical indicators for evaluating maintenance safety and efficiency. The paper concludes that integrating occupational safety into every stage of mechanical maintenance can contribute to a safer working environment, more reliable equipment, reduced operational disruption, and improved organizational performance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Aim: As digital transformation reshapes organizational structures, work, and value creation, understanding its socio-technical foundations becomes critical. Although socio-technical theory offers a lens for analysing the interplay of social and technical elements, its role in digital transformation research remains fragmented. Using the Bostrom and Heinen socio-technical systems model as an analytical framework, this article examines how socio-technical theory is applied in contemporary digital transformation research, identifies dominant patterns across the People, Tasks, Structure, and Technology dimensions, and uncovers conceptual gaps. Methodology: The study followed the PRISMA protocol for systematic literature reviews. Data were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 66 peer-reviewed articles (2020-2026) were analysed, and classified according to socio-technical elements (People, Tasks, Structure, Technology) and modes of theory use (interpretive, analytical, theoretical, discussion). Results: The findings showed that research predominantly focuses on People and Tasks, especially role reconfiguration, work redesign, and human–technology interaction, whilst structural and technological dimensions were less consistently integrated. Socio-technical theory was most often used as an interpretive or theoretical lens, while fewer studies operationalised it analytically. The review revealed uneven theoretical integration and identified gaps related to cross-element alignment, ecosystem-level dynamics, and shifting system boundaries. These findings suggest the need to reinterpret socio-technical theory for digitally complex environments. The review also showed that the depth of theoretical integration varied depending on the focal transformation element, with People-oriented studies applying socio-technical theory more consistently than technology-centred research. Implications and recommendations: The findings highlight the importance of treating digital transformation as a process of continuous socio-technical alignment rather than isolated technological implementation. For researchers, the study identified underexplored relationships between the elements of the Bostrom and Heinen model, calling for more integrative and multi-level research. For practitioners, it emphasised balancing technological investments with organizational structures, work processes, and human capabilities when designing digital transformation initiatives and digital maturity models. Originality/value: This article systematically maps how socio-technical theory is applied in digital transformation research through the Bostrom and Heinen socio-technical systems model, and identifies recurring patterns of theoretical application, highlighting uneven integration across transformation elements, and providing a conceptual framework that synthesizes these relationships. The findings clarify how the model is currently used in digital transformation research and identify areas requiring further conceptual development.

Although the general association between job stressors and health impairments, including effect sizes and directions, has been well researched, the underlying mechanisms of these effects have received relatively less attention. This study developed a cross-theoretical, integrative, mechanism-based stressor–action mechanism model (SAM model) that incorporates action mechanisms (AMs) from different theoretical perspectives to explain the processes through which stressors exert their health-impairing effects. We theoretically derived potential AMs that may underlie the effects of selected job stressors on health impairment. Based on a comprehensive review of meta-analyses on the effects of different job stressors and stress theories in the respective meta-analyses, three overarching processes comprising 14 AMs can be identified: (1) basic-need-related processes: experienced unsafety, fear of renewed threat or violence, perceived loss of control, and autonomy, competence, and relatedness frustration; (2) energetic processes: resource depletion, experience of acute resource loss, experience of resource threat, experience of failed resource investment, depletion of self-control capacity, and recovery impairment; and (3) self-related processes: self-esteem undermining and moral integrity undermining. Specifically, we propose theoretically derived stressor-to-AM pathways for 23 selected job stressors and outline existing empirical evidence for these mechanisms and their relationships with stressors and health outcomes. The SAM further proposes that different job stressors may activate distinct combinations of AMs, resulting in stressor-specific activation profiles; however, the relative distribution of indirect effects across activated AMs remains an empirical question. Importantly, the SAM specifies the stressor-to-AM pathways—that is, which AMs are theoretically expected to be activated by specific stressors—whereas the AM-to-health outcome relationships remain theoretically unspecified. The SAM and its process architecture provide a starting point for understanding the AMs through which job stressors may impair health, as well as for future empirical research on their stressor-specific and cumulative effects, interactions between job stressors and resources, and practical implications for specific person-related and structural interventions.

Airport facilities run continuously, and every fault report, from a jammed baggage belt to a failed chiller or a lift trapping passengers, passes through some form of helpdesk before a technician is dispatched. In many airports this function sits within a work control centre that receives requests, assigns work and tracks completion, yet its potential role in absorbing disruption and coordinating recovery is rarely examined. This paper asks how a centralised helpdesk and work control centre can be organised so that it strengthens the resilience of 24/7 airport facility operations. Thirty refereed journal articles, all dated between 2020 and 2025, are reviewed systematically and integrated across facility management analytics, crisis coordination, resilience engineering and airport operations and synthesised around five themes: request intake and classification, data and performance indicators, situation awareness and digital twins, coordination across teams and organisations, and learning. Two studies anchor the review, one on language-based classification of maintenance requests and one on coordination deficits in crisis governance. The synthesis informs a coordination framework that defines eight core functions of the centre and four operating modes, from normal service to crisis and recovery, with an escalation matrix that specifies triggers, roles, information products and exit criteria. Evidence is supportive for automated request triage and for the value of decentralised yet connected coordination, mixed for digital twins in live operations, and limited for helpdesk-led coordination during airport crises. No primary or proprietary data were used, and the framework is offered as a proposition for empirical testing.
